en: Whichever monk performs manual sexual intercourse, or approves of one doing so; whichever monk causes a limb to move by means of a stick, a leaf-stalk, a finger, or a probe, or approves of one doing so; whichever monk massages or rubs a limb, or approves of one massaging or rubbing it.
Whichever monk should anoint or smear a limb with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or should approve of one who is anointing or smearing it;
whichever monk should rub or scrub a limb with *kakkola*, lodhra, lotus-powder, bath-powder, soap-powder, cosmetic powder, or scented powder, or should approve of one who is rubbing or scrubbing it.
Whichever monk washes or rinses a limb with cold water or warm water, or approves of one who is washing or rinsing it;
whichever monk scrapes a limb, or approves of one who is scraping it;
whichever monk licks a limb, or approves of one who is licking it.
Whichever monk causes a non-living (acitta) liquid to flow into any part of his body and then wipes away the white particles (sukkapoggala), or approves of one who does so;

whichever monk smells a scent placed on something living (sacittapaïṭṭhiya) or approves of one who smells it; whichever monk has a footpath, a bridge, or a handrail made by a member of another sect or a householder, or approves of one who has them made.
Whichever monk has a water-strainer made, or causes it to be made, by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, he commits an offense of expiation.

Whichever monk has a broom or a broom-handle made, or causes it to be made, by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, he commits an offense of expiation. Whichever monk has a needle-case, a cord, or a floor-covering made, or causes it to be made, by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, he commits an offense of expiation.

Whichever monk has a needle sharpened by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or causes it to be sharpened, or approves of its being done; whichever monk has a pair of scissors sharpened by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or causes it to be sharpened, or approves of its being done; whichever monk has a nail-cutter sharpened by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or causes it to be sharpened, or approves of its being done.
Whichever monk has ear-cleaning instruments made, or causes them to be made, by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of such making;
whichever monk has a needle made for no purpose, or causes one to be made, or approves of its being made;
whichever monk has a pair of scissors made for no purpose, or causes one to be made, or approves of its being made.

Whichever monk causes a nail-cutter to be made for no purpose, or approves of one being made, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk causes an ear-cleaner to be made for no purpose, or approves of one being made, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk causes a needle to be made contrary to the rule, or approves of one being made, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk causes a tooth-stick to be made improperly, or approves of one being made improperly; whichever monk causes a nail-cutter to be made improperly, or approves of one being made improperly; whichever monk causes an ear-cleaner to be made improperly, or approves of one being made improperly.
Whichever monk, having had a needle made for his own sake, gives it to another or approves of another giving it, commits an offense.
Whichever monk, having had a pair of scissors made for his own sake, gives it to another or approves of another giving it, commits an offense.
Whichever monk, having had a nail-cutter made for his own sake, gives it to another or approves of another giving it, commits an offense.

Whichever monk, having had a pair of ear-cleaners made for his own sake, gives them to another or approves of another giving them, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk, having had a needle borrowed on loan with the thought "I will sew a garment," sews a shoe or approves of another sewing it, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk, having had a pair of scissors borrowed on loan with the thought "I will cut a garment," cuts a shoe or approves of another cutting it, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk, having taken a loaned nail-cutter with the thought "I will cut my nails," performs the extraction of a thorn (surgery) or approves of one performing it; whichever monk, having taken a loaned ear-cleaner with the thought "I will remove ear-wax," removes tooth-tartar or nail-dirt or approves of one removing it;
whichever monk returns a needle improperly or approves of one returning it improperly.

Whichever monk returns a tooth-stick (*pippalaga*) in an improper manner, or approves of one who returns it in an improper manner; whichever monk returns a nail-cutter (*nahacchēyaṇaga*) in an improper manner, or approves of one who returns it in an improper manner; whichever monk returns an ear-cleaner (*kaṇṇasōhaṇaga*) in an improper manner, or approves of one who returns it in an improper manner.

Whatever monk causes a bronze vessel, a wooden vessel, or an earthenware vessel to be polished, shaped, or cleaned by a member of another sect or a householder—even if it is only slightly—for his own use, knowing and being mindful that this is not permitted, he who lends it to one another, or consents to another lending it, commits an offense.

Whatever monk causes a staff, a walking stick, a cleaning brush, or a bamboo needle to be rubbed, fixed, or polished by a member of another sect or a householder—even for his own use—it is not permissible, even in the slightest, for him to knowingly and intentionally provide such items to one another, nor to approve of such an act.

Whatever monk smooths down a single repair patch on a bowl, or approves of one who does so, [he commits an offense]. Whatever monk smooths down more than three repair patches on a bowl, or approves of one who does so, [he commits an offense].
Whichever monk ties his foot-rope in a manner contrary to the rule, or approves of one who is tying it so, commits an offense.

Whichever monk ties his foot-rope with only a single tie, or approves of one who is tying it so, commits an offense. Whichever monk ties his foot-rope with more than three ties, or approves of one who is tying it so, commits an offense.

Whichever monk wears a foot-binding strap for more than one and a half months, or approves of another wearing it, commits an offense. Whichever monk gives a single patch for a robe, or approves of another giving it, commits an offense. Whichever monk gives more than three patches for a robe, or approves of another giving them, commits an offense.

Whichever monk sews a robe without following the proper procedure, or approves of one who is so sewing, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk makes a single-folded knot on a robe, or approves of one who is making it, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk makes three-folded knots on a robe, or approves of one who is making them, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk ties a single fold of a robe, or approves of one who is tying it; whichever monk ties more than three folds of a robe, or approves of one who is tying it;
whichever monk ties a robe in a manner not according to the rule, or approves of one who is tying it.

Whichever monk causes one who is not of that [monastic] class to fetch [a robe], or consents to another doing so; whichever monk keeps a robe that has been acquired in excess for more than one and a half months, or consents to another doing so;
whichever monk causes a householder’s smoke [i.e., household fire] to be cleared away by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or consents to another doing so.

Whichever monk eats food that has been prepared with putrid matter, or approves of one who so eats, by practicing such an act he incurs a monthly penance (parihāra-ṭṭhāṇa) which is not to be concealed.

Whichever monk makes a wooden-handled foot-wiper, or approves of one being made; whichever monk takes up a wooden-handled foot-wiper, or approves of one being taken up; whichever monk carries a wooden-handled foot-wiper, or approves of one being carried.

Whichever monk distributes a wooden-handled foot-wiper, or approves of one distributing it, commits an offense of atonement (sātisāra). Whichever monk assigns a wooden-handled foot-wiper [for use], or approves of one assigning it, commits an offense of atonement. Whichever monk uses a wooden-handled foot-wiper, or approves of one using it, commits an offense of atonement.
Whichever monk keeps a wooden-handled foot-wiper for longer than one and a half months, or approves of one who keeps it so, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk causes a wooden-handled foot-wiper to be washed, or approves of one who causes it to be washed, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk smells a scent not fixed upon an insentient object, or approves of one who smells it so, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk himself constructs a footpath, a bridge, or a handhold, or approves of one being constructed, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk himself constructs a water-strainer, or approves of one being constructed, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk himself constructs a carrying-net or a carrying-net with a border, or approves of one being constructed, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk himself makes a needle-case, a cord, or a floor-covering, or approves of one being made, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk himself performs the finishing work on a needle, or approves of it being performed, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk himself performs the finishing work on a pair of scissors, or approves of it being performed, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk himself performs the secondary dressing of a wound that has been washed, or approves of one doing so; whichever monk himself performs the secondary dressing of an ear-cleaning instrument, or approves of one doing so; whichever monk speaks harsh words that are light [in gravity], or approves of one speaking them.
Whichever monk speaks a minor falsehood, or approves of one who speaks it; whichever monk takes what is not given as a minor thing, or approves of one who takes it;
whichever monk rinses or washes his hands, feet, ears, eyes, teeth, nails, or face with cold water or warm water as a minor thing, or approves of one who rinses or washes them.

Whichever monk wears skins that are whole, or approves of one who wears them; whichever monk wears garments that are whole, or approves of one who wears them; whichever monk wears garments that are uncut, or approves of one who wears them.

Whichever monk himself rubs, polishes, or cleanses a gourd-bowl, a wooden bowl, or an earthenware bowl, or approves of one who is rubbing, polishing, or cleansing them—[he commits an offense]. Whichever monk himself rubs, polishes, or cleanses a staff, a walking stick, a tooth-stick, or a bamboo needle, or approves of one who is rubbing, polishing, or cleansing them—[he commits an offense].

Whichever monk wears an alms-bowl sought for himself, or approves of one who wears it; whichever monk wears an alms-bowl sought for another, or approves of one who wears it; whichever monk wears an alms-bowl sought for its excellence, or approves of one who wears it.

Whichever monk uses an alms-bowl seeking strength, or approves of one who uses it; whichever monk uses an alms-bowl seeking flavor, or approves of one who uses it; whichever monk eats the first morsel of food from a meal that has been prepared, or approves of one who so eats.

Whichever monk eats regular alms-food, or approves of one who is eating it, commits an offense. Whichever monk eats a non-increased portion of regular alms-food, or approves of one who is eating it, commits an offense. Whichever monk eats a separate portion of regular alms-food, or approves of one who is eating it, commits an offense.
Whichever monk eats a meal that is not a portion for an increase, or approves of one who so eats; whichever monk dwells in a residence during the rainy season, or approves of one who so dwells;
whichever monk establishes intimacy before or after [the rains], or approves of one who so establishes intimacy.

Whichever monk, whether staying [in one place] or residing [there], while traveling from village to village, enters beforehand or afterwards for the sake of alms-seeking those families with whom he was previously acquainted or subsequently became acquainted; or whoever approves of such an entry. Whichever monk, together with a member of another sect or a householder—whether one who is exempt from restrictions or not—enters or exits a householder’s family for the purpose of alms-seeking; or whoever approves of such an entry or exit.

Whichever monk, whether he himself is one who has undergone the probationary period (*parihārika*) or not, goes out with or enters along with a follower of another sect or a householder—whether that person is one who has undergone the probationary period or not—or approves of such a person going out or entering, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk, whether he himself is one who has undergone the probationary period or not, travels from village to village together with followers of other sects or householders—whether they have undergone the probationary period or not—or approves of such traveling, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk, having received some kind of food, eats what is fragrant and fragrant and discards what is foul-smelling and foul-smelling, or approves of one who so discards it; whichever monk, having received some kind of drink, sips what is flavorful and flavorful and discards what is astringent and astringent, or approves of one who so discards it.

Whichever monk, having received a pleasing variety of food, should leave it aside when he is suffering from great distress, without having asked or invited those fellow monks who are living nearby—being of the same communion, of like mind, and not excluded—if he disposes of it or consents to its disposal;
whichever monk takes alms-food belonging to a householder, or consents to one taking it; whichever monk eats alms-food belonging to a householder, or consents to one eating it.

Whichever monk enters a household belonging to a layperson without having informed them, without having asked permission, and without having sought their consent, solely for the purpose of alms-gathering, or approves of one who so enters;
whichever monk, through dependence on a layperson, repeatedly solicits solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacies, or approves of one who so solicits;
whichever monk keeps a bed or bedding belonging to the rainy-season retreat beyond the *pajjosavaṇā* (the termination of the rains), or approves of one who so keeps it.
Whichever monk uses a bed or bedding belonging to the rainy-season retreat for longer than ten days, or approves of one who so uses it;

whichever monk, having seen that a bed or bedding—whether for the dry season or the rainy-season retreat—is being used on top [of another], does not have it moved aside, nor approves of one who does not have it moved aside;

whichever monk, having obtained a bed or bedding for temporary use, carries it outside a second time after having already received permission [to use it once], or approves of one who so carries it outside.
Whichever monk, having obtained permission for bedding and furniture belonging to a householder, carries it outside or consents to another carrying it outside;

whichever monk, having obtained permission a second time for bedding and furniture belonging to a householder or for borrowed bedding and furniture, carries it outside or consents to another carrying it outside;
whichever monk, without having returned borrowed bedding and furniture to its owner, sets out on a journey or consents to another setting out on a journey.
Whichever monk, having himself made no arrangement for a bed or bedding belonging to a householder, departs without returning it, or approves of one who so departs;
whichever monk does not search for a borrowed or a householder’s bed or bedding that has been lost, or approves of one who does not search for it;
whichever monk does not inspect even his limited requisites, or approves of one who does not inspect them.
If he uses that [lodging], he incurs a monthly *parihāra-sthāna* offense that must be confessed.

Whichever monk, in guest-houses, in park-dwellings, in the houses of householders, or in hermitages, solicits food, drink, soft food, or delicacy from a follower of another sect or a householder, or consents to one who is soliciting it, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk, at guest-houses, in park-dwellings, in the families of householders, or in hermitages, solicits food, drink, hard food, or soft food from non-believers or householders, or approves of one who so solicits, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk, at guest-houses, in park-dwellings, in the families of householders, or in hermitages, solicits food, drink, hard food, or soft food from non-believing women or female householders, or approves of one who so solicits, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk, at guest-houses, in monastery dwellings, in the households of householders, or in hermitages, solicits food, drink, chewables, or delicacies from female followers of other sects or female householders, or approves of one who so solicits, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk, at guest-houses, etc., when a follower of another sect or a householder has come for the sake of curiosity, solicits food, drink, chewables, or delicacies from them, or approves of one who so solicits, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk, out of curiosity, when non-proponents of other sects or householders have arrived at the guest-quarters, requests food, drink, soft food, or hard food from them, or consents to another who so requests; whichever monk, out of curiosity, when a female follower of another sect or a housewife has arrived at the guest-quarters, requests food, drink, soft food, or hard food from her, or consents to another who so requests.

Whatever monk, out of curiosity regarding those who have arrived or those who are departing, requests food, drink, soft food, or hard food from female members of other sects or householders, or approves of one who so requests it, [commits an offense].

Whatever monk, having refused food, drink, solid food, or delicacy brought and offered by a follower of another sect or a householder at guest-houses, monastic dwellings, the houses of householders, or hermitages, should then repeatedly follow after him, surround him, hover around him, and entreat him for it—or should approve of one who so entreats—is guilty of an offense.

Whatever monk, having rejected food, drink, solid food, or delicacy brought and offered by a non-believer or a householder at guest-houses or even at hermitages, should then follow after him, repeatedly following him, surrounding him, repeatedly surrounding him, pursuing him, repeatedly pursuing him, and thus solicit him for it—or should approve of one who so solicits him.

Whatever monk, having refused food, drink, solid food, or delicacy brought and offered by a non-believer or a householder at guest-houses or even at hermitages, should thereafter follow after him repeatedly, surround him repeatedly, press him repeatedly, and solicit [the gift], or should approve of one who is so soliciting.

Whichever monk, having refused food, drink, solid food, or delicacy brought and offered by a follower of another sect or a householder at guest-houses or even at lodgings for travelers, subsequently pursues that very person again and again, surrounds him repeatedly, hovers around him repeatedly, and solicits [the gift], or consents to one who is so soliciting;
or whichever monk, having entered a householder’s family for alms and being turned away, enters that same family a second time, or consents to one who is entering it.
Whichever monk, by looking out for a communal feast (*saṅkhaḍī*), accepts food, drink, solid food, or delicacy, or approves of one who is so accepting, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk, having entered a householder’s family for the purpose of alms-gathering, accepts food, drink, solid food, or delicacy brought and offered from beyond the interval of three houses, or approves of one who is so accepting, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk rubs or cleans his own feet, or approves of one who is so rubbing or cleaning them, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk massages or rubs his own feet, or approves of one who is massaging or rubbing them; whichever monk anoints or smears his own feet with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or approves of one who is anointing or smearing them; whichever monk sprinkles or rubs his own feet with lodhra, kakka, powder, or cosmetic paste, or approves of one who is sprinkling or rubbing them.
Whichever monk washes or rinses his own feet with cold water or warm water, or approves of one who is washing or rinsing them;
whichever monk fans or colors his own feet, or approves of one who is fanning or coloring them;
whichever monk rubs or wipes his own body, or approves of one who is rubbing or wiping it.

Whichever monk should massage or rub his own body, or should approve of one who is massaging or rubbing it; whichever monk should anoint or smear his own body with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or should approve of one who is anointing or smearing it; whichever monk should sprinkle or rub his own body with lodhra, kakka, powder, or cosmetic paste, or should approve of one who is sprinkling or rubbing it.
Whichever monk sprinkles or washes his own body with cold water or warm water, or approves of one who is sprinkling or washing it;
whichever monk fans or colors his own body, or approves of one who is fanning or coloring it; whichever monk rubs or wipes a wound on his own body, or approves of one who is rubbing or wiping it.

Whichever monk massages or rubs his own body, or approves of one who is massaging or rubbing it, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk anoints or smears his own body with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or approves of one who is anointing or smearing it, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk sprinkles or rubs his own body with lodhra, kakka, powder, or cosmetic paste, or approves of one who is sprinkling or rubbing it, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk should wash or rinse a wound on his own body with cold water or warm water, or should approve of another doing so;
whichever monk should blow upon or dust a wound on his own body, or should approve of another doing so.

Whichever monk, with any kind of sharp instrument, cuts or lances a boil, a carbuncle, an ulcer, a fistula, or an abscess on his own body, or approves of one who is cutting or lancing it, [commits an offense].

Whatever monk, having cut or incised a boil, a carbuncle, a sore, a fissure, or a fistula on his own body with any kind of sharp instrument, should extract pus or blood, or cleanse it; or should approve of one who is extracting or cleansing it—[this is an offense].

Whatever monk, having cut or incised a boil, a carbuncle, an ulcer, a fistula, or an abscess on his own body with any kind of sharp surgical instrument, and having extracted or purified the pus or blood, should wash or rinse it with cold water or hot water, or should approve of another doing so, [commits an offense].

Whatever monk, having cut or incised a boil, a carbuncle, a rash, a sore, or a fistula on his own body with any kind of sharp instrument, and having extracted or purified the pus or blood, should then wash or rinse it with cold or warm water, or should smear or anoint it with any kind of ointment—whether he does so himself or approves of another doing so.

Whatever monk, having cut or incised a boil, a carbuncle, a rash, a sore, or a fistula on his own body with any kind of sharp instrument, and having extracted or purified the pus or blood, and having washed or rinsed it with cold water or warm water, and having smeared or anointed it with any kind of ointment, such as oil, ghee, fat, or butter, and having massaged or rubbed it with these—whether he does so himself or approves of another doing so—is guilty of an offense.

Whatever monk, having cut or incised a boil, a carbuncle, an ulcer, a fistula, or a hemorrhoid on his own body with any kind of sharp instrument, and having extracted or purified the pus or blood, and having washed or rinsed it with cold or warm water, and having smeared or anointed it with any kind of ointment, and having rubbed or massaged it with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, and having fumigated or deeply fumigated it with any kind of incense—should approve of such an act.

Whichever monk repeatedly inserts and extracts from his own anus or vagina a finger, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk trims or arranges his own long nails, or approves of one who trims or arranges them; whichever monk trims or arranges the long hair on his own shins, or approves of one who trims or arranges it.

Whichever monk should trim or arrange his own long pubic hairs, or approve of another who trims or arranges them; whichever monk should trim or arrange his own long eyelashes, or approve of another who trims or arranges them; whichever monk should trim or arrange his own long armpit hairs, or approve of another who trims or arranges them.

Whichever monk should shave or trim his own long body hairs, or should approve of one who is shaving or trimming them; whichever monk should rub or scrub his own teeth, or should approve of one who is rubbing or scrubbing them;
whichever monk should rinse or wash his own teeth, or should approve of one who is rinsing or washing them.

Whichever monk fans or colors his own teeth, or approves of one who fans or colors them, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk rubs or wipes his own thighs, or approves of one who rubs or wipes them, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk massages or kneads his own thighs, or approves of one who massages or kneads them, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk should massage or rub his own limbs with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or should approve of another doing so; whichever monk should sprinkle or rub his own limbs with lodhra, kakka, powder, or cosmetic paste, or should approve of another doing so.
Whichever monk sprinkles or washes his own body with cold water or warm water, or approves of one who is sprinkling or washing it, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk fans or colors his own body, or approves of one who is fanning or coloring it, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk should trim or arrange his own long upper-lip hairs, or should approve of one who trims or arranges them; [whichever monk should trim or arrange his own long nose hairs, or should approve of one who trims or arranges them];
whichever monk should trim or arrange his own long eyelashes, or should approve of one who trims or arranges them.
Whichever monk should rub his own eyes or wipe them, or should approve of one who is rubbing or wiping them;

whichever monk should massage his own eyes or rub them, or should approve of one who is massaging or rubbing them; whichever monk should anoint his own eyes or smear them with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or should approve of one who is anointing or smearing them.

Whichever monk should rub or scrub his own eyes with lodhra, or with a medicinal paste, or with powder, or with color; or should approve of one who is rubbing or scrubbing them—[he commits an offense]. Whichever monk should wash or rinse his own eyes with cold water or warm water; or should approve of one who is washing or rinsing them—[he commits an offense].
Whichever monk should blow upon or color his own eyes; or should approve of one who is blowing upon or coloring them—[he commits an offense].
Whichever monk should pluck or arrange his own long eyebrow hairs, or should approve of one who plucks or arranges them;
whichever monk should pluck or arrange his own long body hairs, or should approve of one who plucks or arranges them;
whichever monk should remove or clean his own eye-wax, ear-wax, tooth-dirt, or nail-dirt, or should approve of one who removes or cleans them.

Whichever monk should remove or cleanse sweat, dirt, mud, or filth from his own body, or should approve of one who is removing or cleansing it; whichever monk, while traveling from village to village, should have a head-covering made for himself, or should approve of one who is having it made; whichever monk should have a charm-thread made of fine cotton, woolen cotton, *poṇḍa* cotton, or *amila* cotton, or should approve of one who is having it made.

Whichever monk disposes of feces or urine in a house, or at the entrance of a house, or at the door of a house, or at the side-door of a house, or on the eaves of a house, or in the courtyard of a house, or at the latrine of a house, or who approves of one disposing of them; whichever monk disposes of feces or urine in a charnel-house, or on the ashes of a charnel-house, or on the funeral pillar of a charnel-house, or in the resting place of a charnel-house, or in the cave of a charnel-house, or on the sacrificial ground of a charnel-house, or at the latrine of a charnel-house, or who approves of one disposing of them.

Whichever monk disposes of feces or urine on a charcoal fire, or on an alkaline fire, or on a body-fire, or on a chaff fire, or on a husk fire, or approves of one who so disposes of them; whichever monk disposes of feces or urine on a plastered floor, or on a muddy place, or on a place covered with dew, or approves of one who so disposes of them.
Whichever monk disposes of feces or urine in new cow-dung pits, in rivers, or in clay mines—whether they are currently being used or not being used—and approves of one who so disposes of them;
or whichever monk disposes of feces or urine on the roots of an *umbara* tree, a *naggoha* tree, an *asottha* tree, or a *pilakkhu* tree, and approves of one who so disposes of them.

Whichever monk disposes of feces or urine in a sugarcane grove, or a sal grove, or a safflower grove, or a cotton grove, or approves of one who so disposes of them; whichever monk disposes of feces or urine in a ḍāgavacca grove, or a sāgavacca grove, or a mūlavacca grove, or a *kotthumbhari* grove, or a salt-plant grove, or a *jīraya* grove, or a *damaṇaga* grove, or a *marugaha* grove, or approves of one who so disposes of them.

Whichever monk disposes of feces or urine in a grove of *aśoka* trees, or a grove of *saptaparṇa* trees, or a grove of *campaka* trees, or a grove of *cūta* (mango) trees, or in any other such places consisting of leaf-huts, flower-huts, fruit-huts, or shade-huts, or whoever approves of one so disposing of them;

whichever monk, being pressed by the need for feces or urine at night or at twilight, having disposed of his feces or urine in his own vessel or in another's vessel, continues to delay until the sun has risen, or whoever approves of one so delaying—[these commit an offense].
By practicing that, one incurs a monthly *parihāra-sthāna* (offense requiring probation) that has been declared.
Whichever monk makes a king his servant, or approves of one who is making him his servant, [incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense].
Whichever monk causes a king to be brought [to him], or approves of one who is causing him to be brought, commits an offense.
Whichever monk causes a king to be sent away, or approves of one who is sending him away, commits an offense.
Whichever monk causes a royal guard to be brought [to him], or approves of one who is bringing him, commits an offense.

Whichever monk causes a royal guard to be made into a fire-brand, or approves of one who is making him into a fire-brand; whichever monk causes a royal guard to be made into a torch, or approves of one who is making him into a torch; whichever monk causes a city guard to be made into a fire-brand, or approves of one who is making him into a fire-brand.

Whichever monk causes a city guard to be made a slave, or approves of one who is making him a slave; whichever monk causes a city guard to be made a slave, or approves of one who is making him a slave; whichever monk causes a town guard to be made a slave, or approves of one who is making him a slave.

Whichever monk causes a city guard to be treated as a fire-brand, or approves of one who so treats him; whichever monk causes a city guard to be treated as a corpse, or approves of one who so treats him; whichever monk causes a regional guard to be treated as a fire-brand, or approves of one who so treats him.
Whichever monk makes a regional protector a deity, or approves of one who does so;
whichever monk makes a regional protector a god, or approves of one who does so;
whichever monk makes a universal protector a deity, or approves of one who does so.
Whichever monk makes a "fire" out of what is protected by all [means of preservation], or approves of one who does so;
whichever monk makes a "charcoal" out of what is protected by all, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk consumes medicinal herbs that have been kept whole, or approves of one who does so.
Whichever monk eats food that has not been given by his teachers (ācāryas) or preceptors (upādhyāyas), or approves of one who so eats;

whichever monk, without knowing, without asking, and without seeking out, enters beforehand for the purpose of alms-gathering at families designated as "storage-families" (ṭhavaṇa-kula), or approves of one who so enters; whichever monk enters the residence of the nuns (nirgranthīs) contrary to the rule, or approves of one who so enters.
Whichever monk places a staff, a walking stick, a broom, a mouth-cloth, or any other kind of accessory on the path by which the nuns arrive, or approves of one who does so;

whichever monk instigates new, previously non-existent legal disputes, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk re-awakens old legal disputes that have already been confessed and settled, or approves of one who does so.

Whichever monk laughs by repeatedly opening his mouth wide, or approves of one who is laughing so, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk gives a walking stick to one who is living apart from the community (pāsattha), or approves of one who is giving it, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk receives a walking stick from one who is living apart from the community, or approves of one who is receiving it, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk gives a companion to one who is indolent, or approves of one giving it, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk accepts a companion from one who is indolent, or approves of one accepting it, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk gives a companion to one who is lazy, or approves of one giving it, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk accepts the company of a lazy monk, or approves of one who accepts it;
whichever monk gives his company to a contentious monk, or approves of one who gives it; whichever monk accepts the company of a contentious monk, or approves of one who accepts it.

Whichever monk gives a companion to one who is overly attached, or approves of one giving such a companion; whichever monk accepts a companion from one who is overly attached, or approves of one accepting such a companion; whichever monk receives solid food, soft food, snacks, or refreshments with a hand that is wet, or moist, or with a bowl, a ladle, or a vessel that is wet or moist, or approves of one receiving them—[commits an offense].

In this manner, twenty-one [cases involving] hands are to be recited. Whatever monk, with a hand that is moist, or dusty, or mixed with clay, or mixed with alkali, or mixed with salt, or mixed with yellow ochre, or mixed with realgar, or mixed with vermilion, or mixed with red chalk, or mixed with white chalk, or mixed with soratthiya, or mixed with cinnabar, or mixed with collyrium, or mixed with lodhra, or mixed with husks, or mixed with flour, or mixed with bulbs, or mixed with roots, or mixed with ginger-juice, or mixed with *ipuiraga*, or mixed with *ukkuṭṭha*, receives—whether by hand, or by a vessel, or by a ladle, or by a bowl—food, drink, chewable food, or delicacy, or approves of one who so receives it.
Whichever monk makes a village guardian his servant, or approves of one who makes him his servant;
whichever monk makes a village guardian his slave, or approves of one who makes him his slave;
whichever monk makes a village guardian his property, or approves of one who makes him his property.
Whichever monk makes a regional guard into a fire-brand, or approves of one who does so;
whichever monk makes a regional guard into a flame, or approves of one who does so;
whichever monk makes a regional guard into a fuel-wood, or approves of one who does so.
Whichever monk makes a boundary-guard into a slave, or approves of one who is making him into a slave;
whichever monk makes a boundary-guard into a debtor, or approves of one who is making him into a debtor;
whichever monk makes a boundary-guard into a servant, or approves of one who is making him into a servant.
Whichever monk makes royal property his own, or approves of one who makes it his own;
whichever monk makes royal property his flame, or approves of one who makes it his flame;
whichever monk makes royal property his substance, or approves of one who makes it his substance.
Whichever monk makes a "fire-protected" [bedding] into a "flame-protected" one, or approves of one who does so;

whichever monk makes a "fire-protected" [bedding] into a "spark-protected" one, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk makes a "fire-protected" [bedding] into a "embers-protected" one, or approves of one who does so.

Whichever monk should rub or wipe one another’s feet, or should approve of one who is rubbing or wiping them; whichever monk should massage or knead one another’s feet, or should approve of one who is massaging or kneading them; whichever monk should anoint or smear one another’s feet with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or should approve of one who is anointing or smearing them.

Whichever monk rubs or scrubs one another’s feet with lodhra, kakkola, powder, or cosmetic paste, or approves of one who is rubbing or scrubbing them; whichever monk rinses or washes one another’s feet with cold water or warm water, or approves of one who is rinsing or washing them;
whichever monk blows on or fans one another’s feet, or approves of one who is blowing on or fanning them.

Whichever monk should rub or wipe the body of another, or should approve of [another] rubbing or wiping it; whichever monk should massage or knead the body of another, or should approve of [another] massaging or kneading it; whichever monk should anoint or smear the body of another with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or should approve of [another] anointing or smearing it.

Whichever monk rubs or scrubs the body of another with lodhra, or with a medicinal paste (kalka), or with powder, or with colorant, or who approves of one rubbing or scrubbing it; whichever monk washes or rinses the body of another with cold water or warm water, or who approves of one washing or rinsing it; whichever monk fumigates or colors a wound on the body of another, or who approves of one fumigating or coloring it.

Whichever monk should rub or wipe a wound on another’s body, or should approve of one who is rubbing or wiping it; whichever monk should massage or rub a wound on another’s body, or should approve of one who is massaging or rubbing it; whichever monk should anoint or smear a wound on another’s body with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or should approve of one who is anointing or smearing it.
Whichever monk, for another’s body, should rub or scrub a wound with lodhra, kakka, powder, or ointment—or should approve of one who is rubbing or scrubbing it—is at fault.

Whichever monk, for another’s body, should rinse or wash a wound with cold water or warm water—or should approve of one who is rinsing or washing it—is at fault. Whichever monk, for another’s body, should fumigate or color a boil—or should approve of one who is fumigating or coloring it—is at fault.

Whatever monk, with any kind of sharp surgical instrument, should cut or lacerate, or should approve of another cutting or lacerating, a boil, a carbuncle, a sore, a wound, or a fistula on one another’s body.

Whatever monk, having cut or incised with some sharp surgical instrument a boil, a carbuncle, a sore, a fistula, or an ulcer on another’s body, should extract pus or blood, or cleanse it—whether he does so himself or approves of one who does so—is guilty of an offense.

Whatever monk, having cut with some sharp surgical instrument a boil, a carbuncle, a sore, a fissure, or a fistula on another’s body, or having extracted pus or blood, or having cleansed it, should wash or rinse it with cold water or hot water—whether he does so himself or causes another to do so—he commits a *sādhika-dukkaṭa*.

Whatever monk, having cut or incised a boil, a carbuncle, a rash, a scab, or a fistula on another’s body with any kind of sharp instrument, and having extracted or cleansed the pus or blood, then washes or rinses it with cold water or hot water, and then anoints or smears it with any kind of ointment—whether he does this himself or approves of one who does so.

Whichever monk, having incised or cut with some sharp surgical instrument a boil, a carbuncle, a sore, a wound, or a fistula on another's body, and having drained or purified it of pus or blood, then washes or rinses it with cold or warm water, and then anoints or smears it with some kind of ointment—such as oil, ghee, fat, or butter—and thus massages or rubs it, or approves of one who so massages or rubs it, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk, having cut or incised a boil, a carbuncle, a sore, a wound, or a fistula on another’s body with any kind of sharp surgical instrument, and having extracted or purified the pus or blood, then washes or rinses it with cold or warm water, or anoints or smears it with any kind of ointment, or rubs or massages it with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or fumigates or deeply fumigates it with any kind of incense—whether he does so himself or approves of another doing so—he commits an offense.
Whichever monk, having repeatedly inserted either intestinal worms or stomach worms into another’s finger, causes them to be pulled out, or approves of one doing so;

whichever monk cuts or trims another’s long toenails, or causes them to be cut or trimmed, or approves of one doing so; whichever monk cuts or trims another’s long hairs on the shins, or causes them to be cut or trimmed, or approves of one doing so.

Whichever monk plucks or arranges the long pubic hairs of another, or approves of one who plucks or arranges them; whichever monk plucks or arranges the long eyelashes of another, or approves of one who plucks or arranges them; whichever monk plucks or arranges the long armpit hairs of another, or approves of one who plucks or arranges them.

Whichever monk should pluck or arrange the long body hairs of another, or should approve of another plucking or arranging them; whichever monk should rub or scrub the teeth of another, or should approve of another rubbing or scrubbing them; whichever monk should rinse or wash the teeth of another, or should approve of another rinsing or washing them.
Whichever monk should blow on or color each other’s teeth, or should approve of one who is blowing on or coloring them;
whichever monk should rub or wipe each other’s thighs, or should approve of one who is rubbing or wiping them;
whichever monk should massage or knead each other’s thighs, or should approve of one who is massaging or kneading them.

Whichever monk anoints or smears one another’s limbs with oil, ghee, fat, or butter—or approves of another doing so; whichever monk rubs or massages one another’s limbs with lodhra, kakkola, powder, or cosmetic paste—or approves of another doing so.

Whichever monk, for another, should sprinkle or wash with cold water or hot water while standing; or whoever approves of one who is sprinkling or washing [another] while standing—[commits an offense]. Whichever monk, for another, should blow upon or fan [another] while standing; or whoever approves of one who is blowing upon or fanning [another] while standing—[commits an offense].

Whichever monk should pluck or arrange the long upper-lip hairs of another, or should approve of one who is plucking or arranging them; [whichever monk should pluck or arrange the long nose-hairs of another, or should approve of one who is plucking or arranging them];
whichever monk should pluck or arrange the long eyelashes of another, or should approve of one who is plucking or arranging them.

Whichever monk should rub or wipe the eyes of another, or should approve of one who is rubbing or wiping them; whichever monk should massage or anoint the eyes of another, or should approve of one who is massaging or anointing them; whichever monk should smear or rub the eyes of another with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or should approve of one who is smearing or rubbing them.

Whichever monk rubs or massages the eyes of another with lodhra, or with a medicinal paste (kalka), or with powder, or with ointment, or who approves of another doing so; whichever monk washes or rinses the eyes of another with cold water or warm water, or who approves of another doing so; whichever monk blows upon or fumigates the eyes of another, or who approves of another doing so.

Whichever monk plucks or arranges the long eyebrow hairs of another, or approves of one who plucks or arranges them; whichever monk plucks or arranges the long body-hair of another, or approves of one who plucks or arranges it; whichever monk removes or cleans sweat, grime, mud, or dirt from the body of another, or approves of one who removes or cleans it.
Whichever monk should remove or clean the eye-secretion, ear-secretion, tooth-secretion, or nail-secretion of another, or should approve of one who is removing or cleaning them;
whichever monk, while traveling from village to village, should provide a head-covering for another, or should approve of one who is doing so;
whichever monk does not inspect the ground for excrement and urine that has been prepared for him, or should approve of one who is not inspecting it.
Whichever monk does not inspect the three places for excrement and urine, or approves of one who does not inspect them, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk disposes of excrement and urine on a small patch of bare ground, or approves of one who so disposes of it, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk disposes of excrement and urine in an improper manner, or approves of one who so disposes of them, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk, having disposed of excrement or urine, does not wipe it away, or approves of one who does not wipe it away;

whichever monk, having disposed of excrement or urine, wipes it away with a piece of wood, a leaf-shredder, a finger, or a stick, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk, having disposed of excrement or urine, does not wash it away, or approves of one who does not wash it away.

Whichever monk, having disposed of excrement or urine, rinses himself right there, or approves of one who is rinsing himself; whichever monk, having disposed of excrement or urine, rinses himself too far away, or approves of one who is rinsing himself; whichever monk, having disposed of excrement or urine, rinses himself more than three bowlfuls, or approves of one who is rinsing himself.

If a monk says to one who is not a *parihārika* (one exempt from communal duties): "Come, venerable sir! You and I shall take solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacies together, and afterwards we shall eat or drink separately," and if he speaks thus or consents to one who speaks thus—by practicing this, he incurs a monthly penance (*māsiya parihāra-ṭṭhāṇa*) which is to be proclaimed.

Whichever monk, standing at the foot of a tree that has living sap, looks forward or looks around, or approves of one who is looking forward or looking around; whichever monk, at the foot of a tree that has living sap, makes a bed, a seat, or a place for sitting, or approves of one who is making them; whichever monk, standing at the foot of a tree that has living sap, consumes food, drink, soft food, or solid food, or approves of one who is consuming them.
Whichever monk, standing at the foot of a tree with living sapwood, disposes of feces or urine, or approves of one who does so;

whichever monk, standing at the foot of a tree with living sapwood, recites the scriptures, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk, standing at the foot of a tree with living sapwood, instructs in the scriptures, or approves of one who does so.
Whichever monk, standing at the foot of a tree containing living beings, recites the sacred texts himself, or approves of one who is reciting them;
whichever monk, standing at the foot of a tree containing living beings, authorizes the recitation of the sacred texts himself, or approves of one who is authorizing it;
whichever monk, standing at the foot of a tree containing living beings, teaches the sacred texts himself, or approves of one who is teaching them.

Whichever monk, standing at the foot of a living tree, recites the sacred texts or causes them to be recited, incurs an offense of wrong-doing (sātisāra). Whichever monk, standing at the foot of a living tree, reviews the sacred texts or causes them to be reviewed, incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
Whichever monk has his own outer garment sewn by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or causes it to be sewn, incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
Whichever monk makes long threads for his own outer robe (saṅghāḍī), or approves of one who does so;

whichever monk eats the leaves of the *piuṃmanda*, or the leaves of the *paḍōla*, or the leaves of the *billā*, having repeatedly soaked them in cold water or boiled water, or approves of one who does so;

whichever monk, having borrowed a foot-wiping cloth (*pāyapuñchaṇaya*) for a specific occasion, returns it on that very same night with the thought, "I shall return it," yet returns it after [the period] has passed, or approves of one who does so.

Whichever monk, having borrowed a foot-wiping cloth belonging to the Sangha with the thought, "I will return it tomorrow," returns it that very night, or approves of one who returns it, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk, having borrowed a foot-wiping cloth belonging to a householder with the thought, "I will return it tomorrow," returns it that very night, or approves of one who returns it, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk, having borrowed a foot-wiping cloth belonging to a householder with the thought, "I will return it tomorrow," returns it that very night, or approves of one who returns it, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk, having borrowed a staff, a walking stick, a tongue-scraper, or a bamboo needle on loan, returns it on the very same night thinking, "I will return it tomorrow," or approves of one who returns it [in that manner];

whichever monk, having borrowed a staff, a walking stick, a tongue-scraper, or a bamboo needle on loan, returns it on the very same night thinking, "I will return it tomorrow," or approves of one who returns it [in that manner].

Whichever monk, having borrowed from a householder a staff, a walking stick, a cleaning brush, or a bamboo needle, intending "I shall return it tomorrow," returns it that very night, or approves of one who returns it—that monk commits an offense.

Whichever monk, having borrowed from a householder a staff, a walking stick, a cleaning brush, or a bamboo needle, intending "I shall return it tomorrow," returns it that very night, or approves of one who returns it—that monk commits an offense.

Whichever monk, having returned a loaned bed or bedding, uses it again without having requested permission a second time—or approves of one who so uses it—is at fault. The same applies when it is kept with a householder.

Whichever monk, having returned a loaned bed or bedding, whether belonging to himself or kept with a householder, uses it again without having requested permission a second time—or approves of one who so uses it—is at fault.

Whichever monk, having not returned a bed or bedding that was either borrowed for a specific occasion or belonging to a householder, uses it a second time without having asked permission again, or approves of one who so uses it;
whichever monk makes long yarn from fine cotton, coarse cotton, *poṇḍa* cotton, or *amilaka* cotton, or approves of one who so makes it;
whichever monk makes wooden poles, bamboo poles, or cane poles that have living sap, or approves of one who so makes them.
Whichever monk carries wooden staffs containing living organisms, up to and including cane staffs, or approves of one who carries them;
whichever monk makes use of wooden staffs containing living organisms, up to and including cane staffs, or approves of one who makes use of them;
whichever monk makes wooden staffs, bamboo staffs, or cane staffs containing living organisms, or approves of one who makes them.

Whichever monk carries variegated wooden staffs, or even rattan staffs, or approves of one who carries them; whichever monk uses variegated wooden staffs, or even rattan staffs, or approves of one who uses them;
whichever monk makes variegated wooden staffs, or bamboo staffs, or rattan staffs, or approves of one who makes them.

Whichever monk carries variegated wooden staffs, or even rattan staffs, or approves of one who carries them; whichever monk uses variegated wooden staffs, or even [uses] them, or approves of one who uses them.

Whatever monk, having entered a new settlement—whether it be a village, a city, a market town, a hamlet, a fortified town, a port, a capital, a hermitage, a dwelling, a commercial center, a crossroads, a royal capital, or a camp—and there accepts food, drink, solid food, or delicacies, or approves of one who so accepts them, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk, having entered a new settlement containing a copper mine, or a bronze mine, or a tin mine, or a lead mine, or a silver mine, or a gold mine, or a gem mine, or a diamond mine, accepts food, drink, chewables, or delicacies—or approves of one who so accepts them—is guilty of an offense.

Whichever monk plays upon his own face as a lute, or approves of one who does so, is guilty of an offense. Whichever monk plays upon his own teeth as a lute, or approves of one who does so, is guilty of an offense.
Whichever monk makes a "lute-sound" with his armpits, or approves of one who does so;
whichever monk makes a "lute-sound" with his nose, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk makes a "lute-sound" with his armpits, or approves of one who does so.

Whichever monk plays with his hands as a lute, or approves of one who does so, commits an offense. Whichever monk plays with his nails as a lute, or approves of one who does so, commits an offense. Whichever monk plays with his alms-bowl as a lute, or approves of one who does so, commits an offense.

Whichever monk makes a flower-lute, or approves of one being made, commits an offense. Whichever monk makes a fruit-lute, or approves of one being made, commits an offense. Whichever monk makes a seed-lute, or approves of one being made, commits an offense.

Whichever monk makes a lute of green plants, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk plays a lute of the mouth, or approves of one who plays it; whichever monk plays a lute of the teeth, or approves of one who plays it.

Whichever monk plays the "armpit-lute" (uṭṭha-vīṇiya), or approves of one who plays it; whichever monk plays the "nose-lute" (nāsā-vīṇiya), or approves of one who plays it; whichever monk plays the "armpit-lute" (kakkha-vīṇiya), or approves of one who plays it.

Whichever monk plays hand-lutes, or approves of one who is playing them; whichever monk plays foot-lutes, or approves of one who is playing them; whichever monk plays bowl-lutes, or approves of one who is playing them.

Whichever monk plays a flower-lute, or causes one to play it, or approves of one who plays it; whichever monk plays a fruit-lute, or causes one to play it, or approves of one who plays it; whichever monk plays a seed-lute, or causes one to play it, or approves of one who plays it.
Whichever monk causes green plants to be plucked, or approves of one who is plucking them;
whichever monk enters a bed that has been designated for him, or approves of one who is entering it;
whichever monk enters a bed that is under a formal agreement, or approves of one who is entering it.

Whichever monk enters a bed that has been prepared, or approves of one entering it, commits an offense. Whichever monk says, "There is no need for the practice of communal sharing," or approves of one saying so, commits an offense.

Whichever monk repeatedly breaks up and discards a water-strainer made of nettle-fiber, or a wooden vessel, or an earthenware vessel, provided it is sufficient, sturdy, durable, and fit for use, or approves of one doing so, commits an offense.

Whichever monk repeatedly cuts up and discards a robe, an alms-bowl, a blanket, or a foot-wiping cloth that is sufficient, durable, lasting, and fit for use—or whoever approves of one who so discards them; whichever monk repeatedly breaks and discards a staff, a walking stick, a tooth-stick, or a bamboo needle-case that is sufficient, durable, lasting, and fit for use—or whoever approves of one who so discards them.

Whichever monk wears a dust-remover (*rayaharaṇa*) with handles that exceed the proper measure, or approves of one who wears it; whichever monk makes dust-removers with handles that are too fine, or approves of one who does so;
whichever monk ties the dust-remover with a binding for itching, or approves of one who ties it so.
Whichever monk ties his dust-cloth (rayaharaṇa) in a manner contrary to the rule, or approves of one who is so tying it;

whichever monk provides for the dust-cloth only one tie, or approves of one who is providing such; whichever monk provides for the dust-cloth more than three ties, or approves of one who is providing more than that.

Whichever monk wears a dust-remover (rayaharaṇa) that has not been relinquished, or approves of one who wears it; whichever monk wears a dust-remover that has been cast off, or approves of one who wears it; whichever monk takes hold of a dust-remover, or approves of one who takes hold of it.
Whichever monk places his dust-remover (rayaharaṇa) at the base of his head, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk turns it over, or approves of one who does so—
by indulging in that, he incurs a monthly offense requiring expiation (parihāraṭṭhāṇa), which is openly declared.

Whichever monk solicits his mother’s village for the purpose of sexual intercourse, or approves of one who so solicits; whichever monk performs manual sexual intercourse with her in her mother’s village, or approves of one who so performs it.

Whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with Māuggāma, moves a limb with a stick, a splinter, a finger, or a probe, or approves of one who is moving it; whichever monk massages or rubs a limb for the sake of sexual intercourse with Māuggāma, or approves of one who is massaging or rubbing it.
Whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with a mother-village woman, anoints or smears a limb with oil, ghee, fat, or butter—or approves of one who is so anointing or smearing;

whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with a mother-village woman, rubs or massages a limb with a medicinal paste, lodhra-powder, lotus-powder, bath-powder, bathing powder, cosmetic powder, or scented powder—or approves of one who is so rubbing or massaging.
Whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with Māuggāma, should wash or rinse a limb with cold water or warm water, or should approve of one who is washing or rinsing it;
whichever monk should sprinkle a limb with Māuggāma for the sake of sexual intercourse, or should approve of one who is sprinkling it;
whichever monk should sniff a limb with Māuggāma for the sake of sexual intercourse, or should approve of one who is sniffing it.

Whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with his mother’s village [women], causes his semen to be discharged into any non-living liquid by inserting a limb, or consents to one who is discharging it;
whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with his mother’s village [women], himself makes an appointment or himself utters it, or consents to one who is making or uttering it;

whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with his mother’s village [women], engages in a quarrel or utters a quarrel, or goes for the sake of a quarrel, or consents to one who is going—[these commit an offense].
Whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with Māuggāma, writes a letter, causes a letter to be written, or goes for the purpose of a letter, or approves of one who is going;
whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with Māuggāma, pierces with a thorn the breast or the back of a nursing woman, or approves of one who is piercing her.

Whatever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with a woman of the Māuggāma clan, having caused her—who is nursing or suckling—to be lifted up by means of a hook, should rinse or wash her with cold water or warm water, or should approve of another doing so, [commits an offense].

Whatever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with a woman of the Mātṛgrāma clan, having caused her—who is nursing or suckling—to be lifted up by means of a hook, and having washed or rinsed her with cold water or warm water, should smear or anoint her with any kind of ointment, or should approve of one who smears or anoints her.

Whatever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with a woman of the Māuggāma clan, having caused her—who is nursing or suckling—to be lifted up by means of a lever, and having washed or rinsed her with cold water or warm water, or having smeared or anointed her with any kind of ointment, or having massaged or rubbed her with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, approves of [another] doing so, [commits an offense].

Whatever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with a mother-village woman, having caused her—who is nursing or suckling—to be lifted up by means of a hook, and having washed or rinsed her with cold water or warm water, or having smeared or anointed her with any kind of ointment, or having massaged or rubbed her with oil, clarified butter, fat, or fresh butter, or having fumigated or deeply fumigated her with any kind of incense—approves of it.
Whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse in Māuggāma, wears entire (unhemmed) garments, or approves of one who wears them;

Whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with a mother-village woman, causes her to sit or lie down upon a termite mound, or on wood inhabited by living beings, containing eggs, containing small creatures, containing seeds, containing moss, containing mold, or covered with insects, fungi, water-moss, mud, spiderwebs, or cobwebs; or whichever monk causes her to sit or lie down upon a lap or a couch; or whoever approves of such an act of causing her to sit or lie down—[commits an offense]. Whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with a mother-village woman, causes her to sit or lie down upon a lap or a couch; or whoever approves of such an act of causing her to sit or lie down—[commits an offense].

Whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse, having caused a woman to sit or lie down on his lap or on a couch, should offer her solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacies, or cause her to consume them, or should approve of one who so offers or causes her to consume them, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse, should cause a woman to sit or lie down in guest-houses, pleasure-gardens, the houses of householders, or dwelling-places of wanderers, or cause her to sit or lie down there, or should approve of one who so causes her to sit or lie down, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with a mother-villager, causes her to sit down or lie down in guest-houses, pleasure-gardens, the homes of householders, or monastic dwellings, and then offers or causes her to consume food, drink, soft food, or delicacies—or approves of one who so offers or causes her to consume them—is guilty of an offense.
Whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with a mother-villager, provides or approves of providing her with any kind of medical treatment is guilty of an offense.
Whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with Māuggāma, takes away unpleasant matter or approves of one who is taking it away;
whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with Māuggāma, takes away pleasant matter or approves of one who is taking it away.

Whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with the mother-village, seizes any kind of animal species or bird species by its foot, wing, tail, or head, and lifts it up, moves it about, or shakes it; or whoever approves of one who lifts it up, moves it about, or shakes it.

Whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse in Māuggāma, inserts a piece of wood, a blade of grass, a finger, or a stick into the urethra of any kind of animal or bird, and moves it, or consents to one who moves it; whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse in Māuggāma, thinking “this is a woman,” embraces, presses against, or kisses any kind of animal or bird, or consents to one who embraces, presses against, or kisses them.

Whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with [the women of] Māuggāma, gives food, drink, soft food, or solid food, or approves of one giving it; whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with [the women of] Māuggāma, receives food, drink, soft food, or solid food, or approves of one receiving it;
whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with [the women of] Māuggāma, gives a garment, a bowl, a blanket, or a broom, or approves of one giving it.

Whichever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse with [the women of] Māuggāma, accepts a robe, an alms-bowl, a blanket, or a broom, or approves of one who accepts them; whichever monk recites the sacred study (svādhyāya) for the sake of sexual intercourse with [the women of] Māuggāma, or approves of one who recites it; whichever monk receives the sacred study for the sake of sexual intercourse with [the women of] Māuggāma, or approves of one who receives it.

Whatever monk, for the sake of sexual intercourse in Māuggāma, makes a gesture with any of his sense organs, or approves of one who does so— by practicing that, he incurs a four-month penance involving forfeiture that is not curable by confession.

Whichever monk, in guest-houses, or in monastery dwellings, or in the homes of householders, or in hermitages, stays alone with a woman, or performs recitation, or consumes food, drink, soft food, or delicacy, or disposes of excrement or urine, or engages in any other ignoble, harsh conversation unbecoming of a śramaṇa—whether he himself does so or approves of one who does so.

Whichever monk, in a park, or in a house in a park, or in a pavilion in a park; or on a road, or in a house on a road, or in a pavilion on a road—being alone with a single woman, either stays there, or engages in ignoble, harsh, and unbecoming conversation for a śramaṇa—he, by consenting to him who so converses, commits an offense.

Whichever monk, in a watchtower, or in a turret, or in a wall, or in a rampart, or in a gate, or in a city-gate—being alone with a single woman, either stays there, or [engages in conversation], up to: he who converses, or consents to him who converses, commits an offense.

Whichever monk, whether in water, on a path through water, on a ford through water, on a riverbank, or in a place where water stands, stays alone with a single woman—[whether he stays, or engages in conversation, or tells improper talk for a recluse]—or approves of one who does so;

whichever monk, in an empty house, in an empty hall, in a ruined house, in a ruined hall, in a gabled house, or in a storehouse, stays alone with a single woman—[whether he stays, or engages in conversation, or tells improper talk for a recluse]—or approves of one who does so.

Whichever monk, alone with a single woman, stays in a grass-hall or a grass-hut, or in a husk-hall or a husk-hut, or in a chaff-hall or a chaff-hut—[whether he stays there or engages in conversation that is unbecoming of a śramaṇa]—or whoever approves of one who so converses.

Whichever monk, alone with a single woman, stays in a carriage-hall or a carriage-hut, or in a cart-hall or a cart-hut—[whether he stays there or engages in conversation that is unbecoming of a śramaṇa]—or whoever approves of one who so converses.

Whichever monk, in a shop, or a shop-house, or a rest-house, or a rest-house for travelers, or a workshop, or a workshop-house, stays alone with a woman—[whether he dwells there, or engages in conversation, or tells improper talk]—or approves of one who is so doing, [that is an offense].

Whatever monk, in a cow-stable, or in a cow-house, or in a great family, or in a great house, stays alone with a woman—whether he dwells there, recites the scriptures, consumes food, drink, soft food, or delicacies, discharges excrement or urine, or engages in any other ignoble, harsh, and unbecoming conversation for a śramaṇa—he incurs an offense; or if he approves of one who does so, he likewise incurs an offense.
Whichever monk, at night or at twilight, speaks with an unmeasured talk while among women, in the company of women, or surrounded by women, or approves of one who so speaks;

whichever monk, while traveling from village to village together with a nun belonging to his own group or another group—whether she is walking in front or he is walking behind her—with his mind dejected, plunged into an ocean of anxiety and grief, face covered by his palms, fallen into a state of afflictive meditation (*ārta-dhyāna*), or approves of one who speaks such talk (which is unfit for a śramaṇa).
Whichever monk causes a leader or a non-leader, a lay follower or a non-follower, to stay within the residence for half a night or for the whole night, or approves of one who so causes them to stay;
whichever monk does not reject that [conduct], nor approves of one who rejects it.

Whichever monk, depending on a leader or a non-leader, a lay follower or a non-follower, causes them to dwell within the residence for half a night or for the whole night, and departs or enters [the village] on their account, or consents to one departing or entering, [commits an offense].

Whatever monk accepts, or approves of another’s accepting, food—whether hard, soft, chewable, or tastable—at the assemblies of kings, Kṣatriyas, or consecrated monarchs; or at *piṇḍanikara* (food-distributions); or at festivals for Indra, Skanda, Rudra, Maheśvara, Bhūta, Yakṣa, Nāga, Dhūma, Caitya, trees, mountains, caves, wells, ponds, lakes, rivers, pools, oceans, or mines; or at other such various kinds of great festivals—if he does so, he commits an offense.

Whatever monk accepts food, drink, solid food, or delicacy from kings, Kṣatriyas, or those consecrated by coronation who are feasting in the upper hall or the upper chamber, or who approves of another’s so accepting it, commits an offense.

Whatever monk accepts food, drink, solid food, or delicacy from kings who are Kshatriyas consecrated by coronation, while they are in a stable for horses, or in a stable for elephants, or in a council chamber, or in a secret chamber, or in a chamber for sexual pleasure, or one who approves of such acceptance.

Whatever monk accepts, or approves of another’s accepting, milk, curds, fresh butter, ghee, molasses, sugar-candy, granulated sugar, raw sugar, or any other kind of foodstuff from the storehouses or hoards of kings, Kshatriyas, or consecrated monarchs, commits an offense.

Whatever monk accepts, or approves of another’s accepting, the alms-food of kings, Kshatriyas, those consecrated as rulers, or the alms-food set aside for them, or mixed alms-food, or alms-food intended for the destitute, or alms-food from a beggar, or alms-food from a mendicant— he, by practicing such a thing, incurs an offense requiring a four-month penance that is not curable [by confession].
Whatever monk takes, or approves of another’s taking, the royal alms-food.
Whichever monk eats royal alms-food, or approves of one who is eating it; whichever monk enters the king’s inner apartments, or approves of one who is entering them;

whichever monk should say to a person of the inner apartments: "O sir, O person of the inner apartments, it is not permissible for us to go out from or enter the king’s inner apartments; therefore, taking this bowl, fetch and give us food, drink, soft food, or delicacy brought out from the king’s inner apartments"—whichever monk speaks thus, or approves of one who speaks thus.

If a royal attendant should say to a monk: "O venerable ascetic, it is not indeed proper for you to go out or enter the royal harem; however, I shall bring a bowl for you and, having brought forth from the royal harem food or even solid refreshment, I will give it to you"—if he agrees to one who speaks thus, or consents to one who is agreeing, [he commits an offense].

Whatever monk accepts, or approves of another’s accepting, the food of a king, a Kshatriya, one consecrated with the royal unction, provided as a gate-keeper’s meal, or as a meal for cattle, or as a meal for a protector, or as a meal for an army, or as a meal for a horse, or as a meal for an elephant, or as a meal for those traveling through a wilderness, or as a meal during a famine, or as a meal during a time of scarcity, or as a meal for beggars, or as a meal for the sick, or as a meal for those who have grown old, or as a meal for guests—[that monk is guilty of an offense].

Whichever monk, without knowing these six places of danger for kings—Kshatriyas, princes, and those consecrated upon the head—and without having asked or sought permission, goes out to or enters a householder’s family for the sake of alms beyond the limit of four or five houses, or approves of one who is going out or entering, namely: a storehouse, a treasury, a drinking hall, a dairy, a granary, or a kitchen; [that monk commits an offense].

Whichever monk, for the sake of even a single glance, intentionally follows or anticipates the path of kings, Kshatriyas, or consecrated monarchs as they are entering or departing, or whoever approves of one who so acts;

whichever monk, for the sake of even a single glance, intentionally follows or anticipates the path of the women of kings, Kshatriyas, or consecrated monarchs, adorned with all their ornaments, or whoever approves of one who so acts.

Whatever monk accepts, or approves of another’s accepting, food, drink, solid food, or delicacy that has gone outside [the city] from the kitchens of kings, or of those who eat meat, or of those who eat fish, or of those who eat flesh, commits an offense.

Whatever monk, having seen some honorific gift intended for a king, accepts that food when the assembly has not yet risen, is not dispersed, and is not broken up—or approves of one who accepts it; or if he should further know: "Today the king, a Kshatriya, is occupied," and yet that monk, in that house, in that place, or in that vicinity of the lay follower, builds a dwelling, performs recitation, consumes food, drink, soft food, or solid food, disposes of excrement or urine, or engages in any other ignoble, harsh speech unfit for a Śramaṇa—or approves of one who so speaks.
Whichever monk accepts food, drink, solid food, or delicacy from kings, Kshatriyas, lords, or consecrated monarchs who have set out on an external expedition, or approves of one who so accepts;

whichever monk accepts food, drink, solid food, or delicacy from kings, Kshatriyas, lords, or consecrated monarchs who have returned from such an external expedition, or approves of one who so accepts.
Whichever monk accepts food, drink, solid food, or delicacy from kings, Kshatriyas, or consecrated rulers who have set out for a bathing festival, or approves of one who so accepts;
whichever monk accepts food, drink, solid food, or delicacy from kings, Kshatriyas, or consecrated rulers who have returned from a bathing festival, or approves of one who so accepts.
Whichever monk accepts food, drink, solid food, or delicacy from kings, Kshatriyas, or consecrated rulers who have set out on a mountain pilgrimage, or approves of another’s so accepting;
whichever monk accepts food, drink, solid food, or delicacy from kings, Kshatriyas, or consecrated rulers who have returned from a mountain pilgrimage, or approves of another’s so accepting.

Whatever monk goes out or enters the residence of Kṣatriya kings who are consecrated by the head-anointing ceremony while that great coronation is taking place, or consents to one who is going out or entering, [commits an offense].

Whatever monk, within one month, goes out or enters, or consents to another going out or entering, more than once or more than twice, into these ten royal capitals designated for the Kshatriya kings of noble lineage who have been consecrated—namely: Campā, Mathurā, Vārāṇasī, Śrāvastī, Sāketa, Kampilla, Kauśāmbī, Mithilā, Hastināpura, and Rājagṛha—he commits an offense.

Whichever monk accepts food, drink, solid food, or delicacy that has been brought out for another by Kṣatriyas, kings, princes, or royal officials who have been consecrated with the coronation of the head, or whoever approves of such acceptance—namely, those who are Kṣatriyas, or kings, or Kurus, or royal appointees.

Whatever monk accepts food, drink, soft food, or delicacy from a king, a Kshatriya, a noble, or one consecrated by coronation, on behalf of another—whether it be for actors, dancers, wrestlers, boxers, fist-fighters, jesters, storytellers, bards, or performers—and approves of such acceptance, [commits an offense].

Whatever monk accepts food, drink, solid food, or delicacy that has been brought out for others by kings, Kshatriyas, or consecrated rulers—whether it be from those who raise horses, elephants, buffaloes, bulls, lions, tigers, boars, camels, deer, dogs, pigs, rams, chickens, partridges, quails, larks, pigeons, swans, peacocks, or pheasants—or approves of one who so accepts it, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk accepts, or approves of another’s accepting, food, drink, or even solid food that has been brought out for kings or those consecrated by coronation belonging to others—such as elephant trainers or horse trainers; whichever monk accepts, or approves of another’s accepting, food, drink, or even solid food that has been brought out for Kṣatriya kings, princes, or those consecrated by coronation belonging to others—such as elephant riders or horse riders.

Whatever monk accepts, or approves of another’s accepting, food or drink that has been brought out for kings or those consecrated by coronation—such as for horse-riders or elephant-riders—is [subject to a fault].
