Whatever monk accepts, or approves of another’s accepting, food or soft food that has been brought out for kings, Kshatriyas, or those consecrated by coronation—whether they be massagers, rubbers, oil-pressers, shampooers, bathers, decorators, holders of the parasol, holders of the fly-whisk, holders of the *haḍappa* (royal insignia), holders of the palanquin, holders of the lamp, sword-bearers, archers, spear-bearers, or lance-bearers—that is a transgression.

Whatever monk accepts, or approves of another’s accepting, food—up to and including sweets—that has been brought out for kings who have been consecrated by sprinkling, such as the rain-makers, the chamberlains, the gatekeepers, or the staff-guardians; that is a *niḥsargika-pāyantikā* offense.

Whatever monk accepts, or approves of another’s accepting, food—whether solid, soft, or sweet—as it has been brought out for kings, Kṣatriyas, or those consecrated by coronation, from such women as: dwarfs, Cīlikas, Vāmanīs, Vaḍabhīs, Babbarīs, Paüsis, Jōṇis, Palhavīs, Īsis, Thārugis, Lāsīs, Laüsīs, Siṁhalīs, Damilīs, Ārabīs, Pulindīs, Pakkaṇīs, Bahalīs, Maruṇḍīs, Sabarīs, or Pārasīs.
By practicing that, one incurs a four-month period of penance (*parihārasthāna*) that is not mitigated.
Whichever monk speaks harshly to a venerable one, or consents to another who is so speaking, [incurs a *nirgarhaṇīya* offense].

Whichever monk speaks harshly to a venerable one, or approves of one who speaks so; whichever monk speaks severe and harsh words to a venerable one, or approves of one who speaks so; whichever monk insults a venerable one with any kind of insult, or approves of one who insults him so.
Whichever monk eats food mixed with the bodies of infinite-sensed beings, or approves of one who is eating it;
whichever monk eats food prepared specifically for him (āhākamma), or approves of one who is eating it; whichever monk explains a present omen, or approves of one who is explaining it.

Whichever monk explains a sign that has not been authorized, or approves of one who explains it; whichever monk carries away a novice, or approves of one who carries him away; whichever monk causes a novice to change his mind, or approves of one who causes him to change his mind.
Whichever monk steals a direction, or approves of one who steals it; whichever monk alters a direction, or approves of one who alters it;

whichever monk causes a person residing outside the monastery to live together [with the Saṅgha] for more than three nights without having had his instruction verified, or approves of one who so causes him to live together.

Whichever monk, having consumed a gift that involves legal complications (*sādhikaraṇa*), which has not been formally relinquished (*aviosaviya*), for which no penance has been performed (*akaḍapāyacchitta*), and which has been distributed or not distributed by another for more than three nights, or who approves of one so consuming it, commits an offense.
Whichever monk says that what is unreleased (*anugghātiya*) is released (*ugghātiya*), or approves of one who says so, commits an offense.
Whichever monk says that what is released (*ugghātiya*) is unreleased (*anugghātiya*), or approves of one who says so, commits an offense.

Whichever monk gives what has been opened as not opened, or approves of one who so gives, commits an offense. Whichever monk gives what has not been opened as opened, or approves of one who so gives, commits an offense.
Whichever monk, having heard and known that something was opened, consumes it or approves of one who so consumes it, commits an offense.
Whichever monk, having heard or known the reason for a formal suspension (*ugghātiya*), continues to eat together with [the suspended monk] or approves of one who so eats, commits an offense.

Whichever monk, having heard or known the intention for a formal suspension (*ugghātiya-saṅkappa*), continues to eat together with [the suspended monk] or approves of one who so eats, commits an offense.

Whichever monk, having heard or known either the formal suspension itself, the reason for the formal suspension, or the intention for the formal suspension, continues to eat together with [the suspended monk] or approves of one who so eats, commits an offense.
Whichever monk, having heard and known that [food] has not been cleared away, partakes of it or approves of one who partakes of it, commits an offense.
Whichever monk, having heard and known the reason why it has not been cleared away, partakes of it or approves of one who partakes of it, commits an offense.
Whichever monk, having heard and known the intention regarding what has not been cleared away, partakes of it or approves of one who partakes of it, commits an offense.

Whichever monk, having heard or known that [an offense] is non-removable (*anugghāiya*), or has a non-removable cause (*anugghāiya-hetu*), or is of a non-removable nature (*anugghāiya-saṅkappa*), partakes [of food] with him or approves of one who so partakes;
whichever monk, having heard or known that [an offense] is removable (*ugghāiya*) or non-removable (*anugghāiya*), partakes [of food] with him or approves of one who so partakes;

whichever monk, having heard or known that [an offense] has a removable cause (*ugghāiya-hetu*) or a non-removable cause (*anugghāiya-hetu*), partakes [of food] with him or approves of one who so partakes.
Whichever monk, having heard or known that [food] is either "with suspension" (*ugghāiya*) or "without suspension" (*anugghāiya*), partakes of it or approves of another's partaking of it.

Whichever monk, having heard or known that [food] is either with suspension or without suspension, or for the purpose of suspension or for the purpose of non-suspension, or that it is intended for one with suspension or intended for one without suspension, partakes of it or approves of another's partaking of it.

Whichever monk, having risen from his vow of fasting, with a mind resolved upon non-eating, while the sun is still up and he has attained freedom from doubt, accepts and eats food, drink, soft food, or solid food, or approves of one who so eats—yet if he should later realize that the sun has not yet risen or has already set, then by discarding what is in his mouth, what is in his hand, and what is in his alms-bowl, and by purifying himself, he does not transgress; whereas he who eats it, or approves of one who eats it, does transgress.

Whichever monk, having risen from his practice, with a mind resolved on non-existence, while the sun is still up, being overcome by doubt regarding himself, accepts and eats solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacy, or approves of one who so eats; yet if he should know: "The sun has not yet risen, or it has already set," then that which is in his mouth, that which is in his hand, and that which is in his bowl—by discarding and purifying these, he does not transgress; but whoever eats them, or approves of one who eats them, [does transgress].

Whichever monk, having risen [at dawn] and with a mind resolved on what is not yet accomplished, being without a prepared place and having fallen into a state of uncertainty, accepts food, drink, chewables, or delicacies and eats them—or approves of one who eats them; but if he should know: "The sun has not yet risen, or it has already set," then whatever is in his mouth, whatever is in his hand, and whatever is in his alms-bowl, by discarding that and purifying himself, he does not transgress; whereas he who eats it, or approves of one who eats it, does transgress.

Whichever monk, having risen from his practice, with a mind resolved on non-attainment, being unsheltered and overcome by doubt, accepts and eats food, drink, soft food, or solid food for himself, or approves of one who so eats—provided, however, that he knows the sun has not yet risen or has already set, and he disposes of what is in his mouth, what is in his hand, and what is in his alms-bowl, purifying them, he does not transgress; but whoever eats it, or approves of one who eats it [under other circumstances], [does transgress].
Whichever monk, at night or at twilight, having vomited up phlegm mixed with food, swallows it back down again, or approves of one who does so;
whichever monk, having heard that a fellow monk is ill, does not go to inquire after him, or approves of one who does not go;
whichever monk, having heard that a fellow monk is ill, goes by a wrong path or a circuitous route, or approves of one who does so.
Whichever monk, when another monk has undertaken the service of a sick person and is not satisfied with his own gains, does not provide for him or approves of one who does not provide for him;

whichever monk, when another monk has undertaken the service of a sick person and suitable medicinal substances for the sick cannot be obtained, does not refuse [to go elsewhere] or approves of one who does not refuse;
whichever monk travels from village to village during the first rains-retreat or approves of one who so travels.

Whichever monk travels during the rainy season retreat when it has been entered upon, or approves of one who travels, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk does not enter upon the rainy season retreat when it is time for entry, or approves of one who does not enter upon it, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk enters upon the rainy season retreat when it is not the time for entry, or approves of one who enters upon it, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk, during the *pajjosavaṇā*, causes even as much hair as a cow’s tail-hair to be pulled out, or approves of one who does so;

whichever monk, during the *pajjosavaṇā*, consumes even a temporary meal, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk, during the *pajjosavaṇā*, performs the *pajjosavaṇā* with one belonging to another sect or a householder, or approves of one who does so.

Whatever monk accepts alms-bowls or robes during the first section on the assembly, or approves of one who so accepts them— by practicing that, he incurs a four-month period of penance for a transgression that is not curable by confession.

Whatever monk has a drinking vessel made—whether of iron, bronze, copper, tin, gold, silver, natural gold, mother-of-pearl, gems, pearls, horn, ivory, teeth, horn-tips, leather, stone, cloth, crystal, conch-shell, or diamond—or causes one to be made, or approves of its being made, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk holds iron vessels, or bronze vessels, or even conch-shell vessels, or diamond vessels, or approves of one who holds them; whichever monk uses iron vessels, or bronze vessels, or even conch-shell vessels, or diamond vessels, or approves of one who uses them; whichever monk makes iron bindings, or bronze bindings, or even conch-shell bindings, or diamond bindings, or approves of one who makes them.

Whichever monk wears iron fastenings, or bronze fastenings, or even shell fastenings, or diamond fastenings, or approves of one who wears them; whichever monk uses iron fastenings, or bronze fastenings, or even shell fastenings, or diamond fastenings, or approves of one who uses them; whichever monk goes more than half a *yojana* away on foot, or approves of one who goes [there].
Whichever monk accepts food brought from beyond half a *yojana* within a dangerous area, or approves of one who so accepts it;
whichever monk speaks in dispraise of the Dharma, or approves of one who so speaks; whichever monk speaks in praise of what is not the Dharma, or approves of one who so speaks.

Whichever monk should rub or wipe the feet of one belonging to another sect or a householder, or should approve of another who is rubbing or wiping them; whichever monk should massage or knead the feet of one belonging to another sect or a householder, or should approve of another who is massaging or kneading them; whichever monk should anoint or smear the feet of one belonging to another sect or a householder with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or should approve of another who is anointing or smearing them.

Whichever monk massages or rubs the feet of another sectarian or a householder with lodhra, kakkola, powder, or cosmetic paste—or approves of one who is massaging or rubbing them—is guilty of an offense. Whichever monk rinses or washes the feet of another sectarian or a householder with cold water or warm water—or approves of one who is rinsing or washing them—is guilty of an offense.

Whichever monk fans or fans with a fan the feet of one belonging to another sect or a householder, or approves of one doing so; whichever monk rubs or wipes the body of one belonging to another sect or a householder, or approves of one doing so; whichever monk massages or rubs the body of one belonging to another sect or a householder, or approves of one doing so.

Whichever monk should massage or anoint the body of one belonging to another sect or a householder with oil, ghee, fat, or butter—or should approve of someone else doing so; whichever monk should rub or scrub the body of one belonging to another sect or a householder with lodhra, kakkola, powder, or cosmetic paste—or should approve of someone else doing so.
Whichever monk causes a member of another sect or a householder to wash or bathe his body with cold water or warm water, or approves of one who is washing or bathing it;

whichever monk causes a member of another sect or a householder to blow on or color his body, or approves of one who is blowing on or coloring it; whichever monk causes a member of another sect or a householder to rub or wipe a wound on his body, or approves of one who is rubbing or wiping it.

Whichever monk massages or rubs the body of a member of another sect or a householder, or approves of one who is massaging or rubbing it; whichever monk anoints or smears the body of a member of another sect or a householder with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or approves of one who is anointing or smearing it.

Whichever monk should smear or rub with lodhra, kakkola, powder, or cosmetic paste a wound on the body of a member of another sect or a householder, or should approve of one who is so smearing or rubbing it; whichever monk should sprinkle or wash with cold water or warm water a wound on the body of a member of another sect or a householder, or should approve of one who is so sprinkling or washing it.
Whichever monk should fumigate or dye a wound on the body of one belonging to another sect or a householder, or should approve of [another] fumigating or dyeing it;

whichever monk should, with any kind of sharp surgical instrument, cut or incise a boil, a carbuncle, an ulcer, a fissure, or a fistula on the body of one belonging to another sect or a householder, or should approve of [another] cutting or incising it.

Whatever monk, having cut or lanced a boil, a carbuncle, a sore, an abscess, or a fistula on the body of a member of another sect or a householder with any sharp surgical instrument, should extract pus or blood, or cleanse it, or should approve of one who is extracting or cleansing it, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk, having extracted or purified the pus or blood of one belonging to another sect (or even up to: of a householder), washes or rinses it with cold water or warm water, or approves of [another] washing or rinsing it—[he commits an offense]. Whichever monk, having washed or rinsed [the wound] of one belonging to another sect or a householder, anoints or smears it with any kind of ointment, or approves of [another] anointing or smearing it—[he commits an offense].

Whichever monk, having smeared or plastered [the body] of another sectarian or a householder with an ointment—whether with oil, ghee, fat, or butter—and having anointed or rubbed it, or approves of one who is anointing or rubbing it; whichever monk, having anointed or rubbed [the body] of another sectarian or a householder with an ointment—whether with oil, ghee, fat, or butter—and having fumigated or perfumed it with some kind of incense, or approves of one who is fumigating or perfuming it.

Whichever monk, having inserted either a worm from food or a worm from excrement into his finger, repeatedly extracts it, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk, for a member of another sect or a householder, trims or shapes long nails on the fingers or toes, or approves of one who trims or shapes them; whichever monk, for a member of another sect or a householder, trims or shapes long hair on the shins, or approves of one who trims or shapes it.
Whichever monk should have the long pubic hairs of a follower of another sect or a householder trimmed or shaped, or should approve of one who is having them trimmed or shaped;
whichever monk should have the long eyelashes of a follower of another sect or a householder trimmed or shaped, or should approve of one who is having them trimmed or shaped;
whichever monk should have the long armpit hairs of a follower of another sect or a householder trimmed or shaped, or should approve of one who is having them trimmed or shaped.

Whichever monk should have the long hair or body hair of a follower of another sect or a householder shaved or trimmed, or should approve of one who is having it shaved or trimmed; whichever monk should rub or scrub the teeth of a follower of another sect or a householder, or should approve of one who is rubbing or scrubbing them;
whichever monk should rinse or wash the teeth of a follower of another sect or a householder, or should approve of one who is rinsing or washing them.

Whichever monk should blow on or color the teeth of another sectarian or a householder, or should approve of one who is blowing on or coloring them; whichever monk should rub or wipe the thighs of another sectarian or a householder, or should approve of one who is rubbing or wiping them; whichever monk should massage or knead the thighs of another sectarian or a householder, or should approve of one who is massaging or kneading them.

Whichever monk should massage or rub with oil, ghee, fat, or butter the limbs of one belonging to another sect or a householder, or should approve of [another] massaging or rubbing them; whichever monk should sprinkle or rub with lodhra, kakkola, powder, or cosmetic paste the limbs of one belonging to another sect or a householder, or should approve of [another] sprinkling or rubbing them.
Whichever monk causes a member of another sect or a householder to wash or rinse his feet with cold water or warm water, or consents to one who is washing or rinsing them;
whichever monk causes a member of another sect or a householder to blow on or fan his feet, or consents to one who is blowing on or fanning them.

Whichever monk should have the long upper-lip hair of a follower of another sect or a householder trimmed or shaped, or should approve of one who is having it trimmed or shaped; [whichever monk should have the long nose-hair of a follower of another sect or a householder trimmed or shaped, or should approve of one who is having it trimmed or shaped.]

Whichever monk should trim or shape long eye-eyelashes for one belonging to another sect or for a householder, or should approve of [another] doing so; whichever monk should rub or wipe the eyes of one belonging to another sect or of a householder, or should approve of [another] doing so; whichever monk should massage or anoint the eyes of one belonging to another sect or of a householder, or should approve of [another] doing so.

Whichever monk should massage or rub the eyes of a member of another sect or a householder with oil, ghee, fat, or butter—or should approve of one who is massaging or rubbing them—[commits an offense].

Whichever monk should sprinkle or rub the eyes of a member of another sect or a householder with lodhra, kakkola, powder, or cosmetic paste—or should approve of one who is sprinkling or rubbing them—[commits an offense].
Whichever monk should wash or rinse the eyes of another sectarian or a householder with cold water or warm water, or should approve of one who is washing or rinsing them;
whichever monk should blow on or color the eyes of another sectarian or a householder, or should approve of one who is blowing on or coloring them.
Whichever monk should trim or arrange the long eyebrow-hairs of a follower of another sect or a householder, or should approve of one who trims or arranges them;
whichever monk should trim or arrange the long body-hair of a follower of another sect or a householder, or should approve of one who trims or arranges it.

Whichever monk should remove or cleanse sweat, dirt, mud, or filth from the body of one belonging to another sect or a householder, or should approve of one who is removing or cleansing it; whichever monk should remove or cleanse the impurity of the eyes, the impurity of the ears, the impurity of the teeth, or the impurity of the nails of one belonging to another sect or a householder, or should approve of one who is removing or cleansing it.
Whichever monk, while traveling from village to village, makes a non-believer or a householder carry his head-cloth, or approves of one who does so;
whichever monk causes himself to be terrified, or approves of one who causes him to be terrified; whichever monk causes another to be terrified, or approves of one who causes another to be terrified.
Whichever monk causes himself to be mocked, or approves of one who is mocking him;
whichever monk mocks another, or approves of one who is mocking another; whichever monk causes himself to be deluded, or approves of one who is deluding him.

Whichever monk causes another to be perverted, or approves of one who is being caused to be perverted; whichever monk makes a facial expression, or approves of one who is making a facial expression; whichever monk makes a prepared departure, a prepared arrival, or a prepared departure-and-arrival in a kingdom that is hostile or rebellious, or approves of one who is doing so.

Whichever monk speaks in dispraise of eating during the day, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk speaks in praise of eating at night, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk, having accepted food, drink, solid food, or delicacy during the day, eats it during the day, or approves of one who does so.
Whichever monk, having accepted food, drink, solid food, or delicacy during the day, eats it at night, or approves of one who so eats;
whichever monk, having accepted food, drink, solid food, or delicacy at night, eats it during the day, or approves of one who so eats;
whichever monk, having accepted food, drink, solid food, or delicacy at night, eats it at night, or approves of one who so eats.
Whichever monk sets aside food, drink, hard food, or soft food when there is no pressing need, or approves of one who so sets them aside;

whichever monk consumes, or approves of another consuming, even a portion the size of a leaf-cup, a grain of rice, or a drop of water, of such food, drink, hard food, or soft food that has been set aside.

Whichever monk, having seen meat or fish, or a heap of meat, or a heap of fish, whether as a gift, a present, or a communal offering, or a portion of *hiṅgu* (asafoetida), or any other such various kinds of food being carried away, should—out of desire for it or thirst for it—cause that night to pass elsewhere, or cause another to pass it elsewhere, or approves of [such an act].
Whichever monk eats a meal provided as a special treat (*niveyaṇapiṇḍa*), or approves of one who eats it.
Whichever monk praises [a donor] according to their whim, or approves of one who praises them.
Whichever monk pays homage according to his own whim, or approves of one who does so, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk ordains, or approves of one who ordains, a leader, a non-leader, a lay follower, or a non-follower who is incapable [of the religious life], [commits an offense].

Whichever monk causes to undergo the formal retreat (upasthāpanā), or approves of one who causes it, a leader, a non-leader, a lay follower, or a non-follower who is incapable [of the religious life], [commits an offense].
Whichever monk performs service with fire, or causes it to be performed, or approves of it doing so;

whichever monk dwells among those who possess robes while he himself possesses robes, or approves of one so dwelling; whichever monk dwells among those who are without robes while he himself possesses robes, or approves of one so dwelling.
Whichever monk dwells among those who possess robes while he is himself without robes, or approves of one who so dwells;
whichever monk dwells among those who are without robes while he is himself without robes, or approves of one who so dwells;
whichever monk eats long pepper or long pepper powder, ginger or ginger powder, rock salt or sea salt, or salt produced from saline soil, or approves of one who so eats.

Whatever monk praises, or approves of one who praises, such foolish deaths as falling from a mountain, falling from a desert plateau, falling into a chasm, falling from a tree; leaping from a mountain, leaping from a desert plateau, leaping into a chasm, leaping from a tree; entering water, entering fire, leaping into water, leaping into fire; consuming poison, inflicting wounds with weapons, death by hanging, death through madness, death by self-starvation, death from internal disease, death by hanging oneself, death by being devoured by vultures, or any other similar kinds of foolish deaths—[he commits an offense].
By practicing that, one incurs a four-month period of penance (*parihārasthāna*) that is not mitigated.

Whichever monk, out of a desire for gain, binds any kind of living being of the mobile class with a grass-noose, a *muñja*-grass noose, a wooden noose, a leather noose, a bamboo noose, a rope noose, or a thread noose— or approves of another binding them— [commits an offense].
Whichever monk, out of compassion, releases [an animal] that is bound by a cord or a snare, or approves of one who does so;
whichever monk repeatedly breaks his vow of renunciation, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk consumes food mixed with small-bodied living beings, or approves of one who does so.
Whichever monk wears skins with the hair on them, or approves of one who wears them;
whichever monk uses a bed of grass, a bed of straw, a bed of cow-dung, a bed of reeds, or a bed of wood that is covered with another cloth, or approves of one who uses it;
whichever monk has a nun’s outer garment sewn by a member of another sect or by a householder, or approves of one who has it sewn.

Whichever monk instigates even a slight injury to the earth-body, or approves of one who is so instigating; likewise, whichever monk instigates even a slight injury to the water-body, the fire-body, the air-body, or the plant-body, or approves of one who is so instigating.
Whichever monk climbs a tree containing living beings, or approves of one who is climbing it.
Whichever monk eats food belonging to a householder, or approves of one who is eating it.
Whichever monk wears a householder’s garment, or approves of one who wears it; whichever monk uses a householder’s bed, or approves of one who uses it;
whichever monk practices medicine for a householder, or approves of one who does so.
Whichever monk accepts, or approves of another’s accepting, solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacy with a hand, a bowl, a ladle, or a vessel that has been pre-washed;

whichever monk accepts, or approves of another’s accepting, solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacy with a hand, or up to a vessel, belonging to householders or members of other sects that has been used for the consumption of cold water.

Whatever monk should, for the sake of eye-pleasure, intentionally prepare—whether he does so himself or approves of another doing so—carvings in wood, paintings, embroideries, ivory work, jewelry, stonework, knotted textiles, woven fabrics, stuffed cushions, patchwork robes, or various other kinds of needlework; ...he commits an offense.

Whatever monk intentionally directs his gaze toward cultivated fields, or embankments, or lotus ponds, or marshes, or waterfalls, or cascades, or tanks, or lotus pools, or oblong ponds, or canals, or lakes, or rows of lakes, or series of lakes for the purpose of seeing them, or who approves of one so directing his gaze—[that monk commits an offense].

Whichever monk intentionally fixes his gaze upon thickets, dense growths, thickets of grass, forests, forest thickets, mountains, or mountain thickets for the purpose of seeing with his eyes, or whoever approves of one who so fixes his gaze; whichever monk intentionally fixes his gaze upon villages, towns, hamlets, market towns, border towns, seaports, cities, mines, caravan halting places, or settlements for the purpose of seeing with his eyes, or whoever approves of one who so fixes his gaze.

Whichever monk, for the sake of seeing with his eyes, fixes his gaze upon a village settlement or even a caravan encampment—or upon the conflagrations of villages or even the conflagrations of caravan encampments—and whoever approves of one who so fixes his gaze;

whichever monk, for the sake of seeing with his eyes, fixes his gaze upon a village being carried away or even a caravan encampment being carried away—or upon the floods of villages or even the floods of caravan encampments—and whoever approves of one who so fixes his gaze;

whichever monk, for the sake of seeing with his eyes, fixes his gaze upon a village being swept away or even a caravan encampment being swept away—or upon the torrents of villages or even the torrents of caravan encampments—and whoever approves of one who so fixes his gaze.
Whichever monk, for the sake of seeing or looking at them, approves of horse-training, elephant-training, camel-training, ox-training, buffalo-training, or pig-training;
or whichever monk, for the sake of seeing or looking at them, approves of horse-fights, elephant-fights, camel-fights, ox-fights, buffalo-fights, or ram-fights.

Whichever monk intentionally looks toward places for horse-races, places for chariot-races, or places for elephant-races for the purpose of seeing them, or approves of one who so looks, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk intentionally looks toward places for royal ablutions, places for storytelling, places for measuring with weights and measures, or places for great performances of dancing, singing, instrumental music, stringed instruments, hand-clapping, rhythmic beating, and the sounding of various musical instruments for the purpose of seeing them, or approves of one who so looks, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk, out of a desire for sight or seeing, [goes to] public spectacles, riots, disturbances, quarrels, enmities, great battles, great conflicts, brawls, or tumults, [he commits an offense].

Whatever monk, with the intention of seeing them, fixes his gaze upon women or men—whether old, middle-aged, or young; whether unadorned or well-adorned; whether singing, playing instruments, dancing, laughing, sporting, or enjoying themselves—at a great festival of various kinds, while they are distributing or consuming abundant food, drink, solid food, or delicacies, or approves of one who so fixes his gaze.

Whatever monk becomes attached, becomes impassioned, becomes greedy, and becomes infatuated with forms belonging to this world or forms belonging to the other world—whether those forms have been seen or not seen, heard or not heard, known or not known—if he approves of one who is becoming attached, impassioned, greedy, or infatuated; [he commits an offense].

Whichever monk, having accepted solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacy during the first watch of the day, causes it to be brought to him during the last watch, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk causes solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacy to be brought from more than half a *yojana* away, or approves of one who does so;
whichever monk, having accepted cow dung by day, applies it to his body by day, or rubs it in, or approves of one who does so.

Whichever monk, having received cow dung during the day, should smear or anoint a wound on his body at night, or should approve of one who smears or anoints it; whichever monk, having received cow dung at night, should smear or anoint a wound on his body during the day, or should approve of one who smears or anoints it;
whichever monk, having received cow dung at night, should smear or anoint a wound on his body at night, or should approve of one who smears or anoints it.
Whichever monk, having accepted ointments during the day, applies or smears them upon a wound on his body during the day—or approves of one who is applying or smearing them—is guilty of an offense.
Whichever monk, having accepted ointments during the day, applies or smears them upon a wound on his body at night—or approves of one who is applying or smearing them—is guilty of an offense.
Whichever monk, having accepted ointments at night, applies or smears them upon a wound on his body during the day—or approves of one who is applying or smearing them—is guilty of an offense.
Whichever monk, having accepted a type of ointment at night, should smear or rub it onto his body at night, or should approve of one who is so smearing or rubbing it;
whichever monk has a robe washed by a member of another sect or a householder, or approves of one who is having it washed;
whichever monk gives food, drink, soft food, or solid food under their supervision, or approves of one who is giving it.

Whatever monk crosses or wades across, or consents to another crossing or wading across, these five great rivers which have been declared, enumerated, and specified— namely, the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Sarayū, the Airāvatī, and the Mahī—
if he does so more than twice or thrice within a month, he incurs a four-month penance of probation (parihāra-ṭṭhāṇa) with suspension.
Whichever monk prepares a standing place, a bed, a seat, or a resting place on bare ground, or approves of one who does so;
whichever monk prepares a standing place, or [bed, seat, or resting place] up to the point of preparing it, on moist ground, or approves of one who does so;
whichever monk prepares a standing place, or bed, seat, or resting place on dusty ground, or approves of one who does so.
Whichever monk stands upon, or up to—cleanses—earth that has been smoothed with clay, or approves of one who does so;

whichever monk stands upon, or up to—cleanses—earth that possesses life, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk stands upon, or up to—cleanses—a stone that possesses life, or approves of one who does so.
Whichever monk makes a bed, or causes one to be made, on a piece of leather with hair on it, or approves of such an act;

whichever monk makes a bed, or causes one to be made, on wood inhabited by living beings—containing eggs, containing creatures, containing seeds, containing sprouts, containing moisture, containing dew, and covered with ant-hills, fungi, water-moss, mud, and spiderwebs—or approves of such an act.

Whatever monk stands, lies down, sits, or stretches out his limbs upon a pillar, a wooden beam, a bamboo pole, a raft, or any other such thing produced from the open air that is poorly fastened, poorly placed, unstable, and shaky—he who does so, or approves of one who does so, commits an offense.

Whatever monk places his standing place, bed, couch, or sitting mat upon a pillar, a wall, a stone, a brick, or any other such thing produced in the open air that is poorly fastened, poorly placed, unstable, and shaky—he, by so doing, or by approving of one who does so, commits an offense.

Whatever monk, on a pillar, a wall, a couch, a bedstead, a gallery, a palace, a floor, or any other such open-air structure that is poorly fastened, poorly placed, unstable, and shaky, stands, lies down, sits, or performs a formal posture—whether he does so himself or consents to another doing so—is guilty of an offense.

Whichever monk teaches, or approves of another teaching, a non-believer (anyatīrthika) or a householder (gṛhastha) a craft, a verse, a legal code, a calculation, a disputation, praise, or the manual for praising;
whichever monk speaks harshly, or approves of another speaking harshly, to a non-believer or a householder;
whichever monk speaks abusively, or approves of another speaking abusively, to a non-believer or a householder.

Whichever monk speaks harshly and severely to one belonging to another sect or to a householder, or approves of one who so speaks; whichever monk threatens one belonging to another sect or a householder with any kind of threat, or approves of one who so threatens; whichever monk performs a rite of sorcery for one belonging to another sect or a householder, or approves of one who performs such a rite.

Whichever monk performs a rite for prosperity (*bhūtikamma*) for one belonging to another sect or a householder, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk explains a riddle (*pasiṇa*) to one belonging to another sect or a householder, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk explains a riddle and its answer (*pasiṇāpasiṇa*) to one belonging to another sect or a householder, or approves of one who does so.

Whichever monk explains, or approves of another explaining, a past omen to one belonging to another sect or to a householder; whichever monk explains, or approves of another explaining, bodily marks to one belonging to another sect or to a householder; whichever monk explains, or approves of another explaining, dreams to one belonging to another sect or to a householder.
Whichever monk employs a spell for those of other sects or for householders, or approves of one who does so, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk employs a mantra for those of other sects or for householders, or approves of one who does so, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk employs a yoga for those of other sects or for householders, or approves of one who does so, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk shows the way to outsiders or householders who are lost, bewildered, or confused—whether he points out the path, points out a breach (sandhi), leads from the path to a breach, or leads from a breach to the path—or whoever approves of one doing so;
whichever monk points out a thief to outsiders or householders—or whoever approves of one doing so;
whichever monk points out a hidden treasure to outsiders or householders—or whoever approves of one doing so.

Whichever monk burns himself with a brazier, or approves of one who burns himself; whichever monk burns himself with a charcoal pit, or approves of one who burns himself; whichever monk burns himself with a sword, or approves of one who burns himself.
Whichever monk burns himself with jewels, or approves of one who burns himself;
whichever monk burns himself with fire, or approves of one who burns himself;
whichever monk burns himself with oil, or approves of one who burns himself.
Whichever monk anoints himself with yeast-leavened paste, or approves of one who does so;
whichever monk anoints himself with fat, or approves of one who does so;
whichever monk performs the remedy of emetics, or approves of one who does so.

Whichever monk performs a purgative treatment as a medical remedy, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk performs emetic and purgative treatments as a medical remedy, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk performs a medical remedy when he is not ill, or approves of one who does so.
Whichever monk pays homage to one who is living in association with the laity, or approves of another doing so, commits an offense.
Whichever monk praises one who is living in association with the laity, or approves of another doing so, commits an offense.
Whichever monk pays homage to one who is living in negligence, or approves of another doing so, commits an offense.
Whichever monk praises one who is indolent, or consents to another praising one who is indolent;
whichever monk pays homage to one who is indolent, or consents to another paying homage to one who is indolent;
whichever monk praises one who is indolent, or consents to another praising one who is indolent.
Whichever monk pays homage to a nun, or approves of one who pays homage to her, commits an offense of wrong-doing.
Whichever monk praises a nun, or approves of one who praises her, commits an offense of wrong-doing.
Whichever monk pays homage to one who is closely associated with nuns, or approves of one who pays homage to her, commits an offense of wrong-doing.
Whichever monk praises one who is closely associated with householders, or approves of one who is praising such a person, commits an offense.
Whichever monk pays homage to one who acts for the sake of gain, or approves of one who is paying homage, commits an offense.
Whichever monk praises one who acts for the sake of gain, or approves of one who is praising such a person, commits an offense.
Whichever monk pays homage to a lay follower (pāsaṇiya), or approves of one who pays homage, commits an offense.
Whichever monk praises a lay follower, or approves of one who praises, commits an offense.
Whichever monk pays homage to a female ascetic (māmaga), or approves of one who pays homage, commits an offense.
Whichever monk praises a *māmaka* (one who says "mine"), or approves of one who praises him, commits an offense involving expiation (*sātisāra*).
Whichever monk pays homage to one who extends his hand in greeting, or approves of one who pays homage, commits an offense involving expiation.
Whichever monk praises one who extends his hand in greeting, or approves of one who praises him, commits an offense involving expiation.
Whichever monk eats food brought by a female messenger, or approves of one who so eats, commits an offense.
Whichever monk eats food brought by a male messenger, or approves of one who so eats, commits an offense.
Whichever monk eats food brought as a sign, or approves of one who so eats, commits an offense.

Whichever monk eats the alms-food of the Ājīvikas, or approves of one who eats it; whichever monk eats the alms-food of wandering mendicants, or approves of one who eats it; whichever monk eats the alms-food of medical practitioners, or approves of one who eats it.

Whichever monk eats alms-food obtained through anger, or approves of one who so eats; whichever monk eats alms-food obtained through pride, or approves of one who so eats; whichever monk eats alms-food obtained through deceit, or approves of one who so eats.

Whichever monk eats food obtained through greed, or approves of one who so eats; whichever monk eats food obtained through sorcery, or approves of one who so eats; whichever monk eats food obtained through incantations, or approves of one who so eats.
Whichever monk eats food obtained through a trade, or approves of one who so eats;
whichever monk eats food consisting of powdered substances, or approves of one who so eats;
whichever monk eats food obtained by means of concealment, or approves of one who so eats.
By practicing that, one incurs a four-month period of penance (*parihārasthāna*) with its suspension lifted.
Whichever monk buys an alms-bowl, causes it to be bought, or accepts one that has been bought and brought to him, or approves of one being accepted, [incurs an offense].
Whichever monk lends out an alms-bowl, causes it to be lent out, or accepts an alms-bowl that is being given after having been brought back from a loan, or approves of one who so accepts it;
whichever monk exchanges an alms-bowl, causes it to be exchanged, or accepts an alms-bowl that is being given after having been brought back from an exchange, or approves of one who so accepts it;
whichever monk accepts an alms-bowl that is seized, ungiven, or brought as a gift, or approves of one who so accepts it.

Whichever monk, having set aside an extra alms-bowl for a group and having designated it for a group, distributes it to one another without having asked that group or informed them, or approves of one who so distributes it.

Whichever monk gives an extra alms-bowl to a junior monk or a junior nun, or to an elder monk or an elder nun—whether they have had their hands cut off, their feet cut off, their ears cut off, their noses cut off, or their lips cut off—or to one who is capable, or approves of one who gives it.
Whichever monk does not give an extra alms-bowl to one who is small or smallish, up to one whose lips are severed and is incapable, or approves of another not giving it;

whichever monk keeps an alms-bowl that is insufficient, unstable, non-durable, and unfit for use, or approves of another keeping it; whichever monk does not keep an alms-bowl that is sufficient, stable, durable, and fit for use, or approves of another not keeping it.
Whichever monk makes a variegated alms-bowl plain, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk makes a plain alms-bowl variegated, or approves of one who does so;
whichever monk, thinking "I have obtained a new alms-bowl," rinses it or washes it with cold water or hot water, or approves of one who rinses or washes it so.

Whichever monk, thinking "this alms-bowl of mine is not new," should—having obtained it—wash or rinse it with cold water or warm water that has been used for many days, or should approve of another doing so; whichever monk, thinking "this alms-bowl of mine is not new," should rub or scrub it with *kakkā* (a type of soap), *loddha* (moss), powder, or dye, or should approve of another doing so.

Whichever monk, thinking "this alms-bowl has been obtained by me as new," rubs it or polishes it with much-day-old *kakkā*, *loddha*, powder, or dye, or approves of one who is rubbing or polishing it;
whichever monk, thinking "this alms-bowl has been obtained by me as foul-smelling," rinses it or washes it with cold water or warm water, or approves of one who is rinsing or washing it.

Whichever monk, thinking "I have received an alms-bowl with a foul odor," should wash or rinse it with much water that has been kept for many days—whether cold water or hot water—or should approve of another washing or rinsing it;
whichever monk, thinking "I have received an alms-bowl with a foul odor," should rub or scrub it with *kakkā*, *loddha*, powder, or colorant—or should approve of another rubbing or scrubbing it.

Whatever monk, thinking "I have obtained an alms-bowl with an unpleasant odor," should rub or scrub it with much country-made *kakkā*, or *loddha*, or powder, or dye; or should approve of one who is rubbing or scrubbing it—[in the same way, if he should smear or anoint it with oil, or ghee, or butter, or fat; or should approve of one who is smearing or anointing it—these four sections are to be recited].

Whichever monk, on ground that is not separated [by a sufficient interval] from living beings down to those supported by moisture—down to being with eggs, down to being with crawling creatures, and being unstable and moving—causes his alms-bowl to be carried or caused to be carried [over it], or consents to another’s doing so;

whichever monk, on moist ground... down to causing his alms-bowl to be carried... or consents to another’s doing so; whichever monk, on dusty ground... down to causing his alms-bowl to be carried... or consents to another’s doing so.
Whichever monk causes his alms-bowl to be heated upon raw, unbaked earth—or [does so] up to the point of approving it;

whichever monk causes his alms-bowl to be heated upon living earth—or [does so] up to the point of approving it; whichever monk causes his alms-bowl to be heated upon living stone—or [does so] up to the point of approving it.
Whichever monk causes an alms-bowl to be brought [or causes it to be washed] upon a surface covered with living beings, up to:

whichever monk causes an alms-bowl to be brought or caused to be washed upon a wooden plank inhabited by living beings, containing eggs, containing small creatures, containing seeds, containing sprouts, containing moisture, containing mildew, and containing moss, fungi, water-lichen, mud, or spiderwebs—whether he does so himself, causes another to do so, or approves of its being done—he commits an offense.

Whichever monk, on a pillar, or on a house-beam, or on a bamboo-pole, or on a water-channel, or on any other such thing growing out of the open air—when it is poorly fastened, poorly placed, unstable, and shaky—if he causes his alms-bowl to be hung there or causes it to be hung by another, or approves of its being so hung or caused to be hung, [he commits an offense]. Whichever monk, on a wooden peg, or on a wall, or on a stone, or on a brick, or on any other such thing growing out of the open air—when it is poorly fastened, and so forth, up to: if he causes it to be hung or causes it to be hung by another, or approves of its being so hung or caused to be hung, [he commits an offense].

Whichever monk causes his alms-bowl to be brought or caused to be brought upon a pillar, a threshold, a couch, a small bed, a gallery, a palace, a floor, or any other such open space that is poorly secured, poorly placed, unstable, and shaky—he incurs a fault.
Whichever monk removes the earth-element from his alms-bowl, or causes it to be removed, or accepts it when it is brought back after having been removed—he incurs a fault.
Whichever monk takes out water from his alms-bowl, or causes it to be taken out, or approves of its being taken out—up to the point of enjoying it;
whichever monk takes out fire from his alms-bowl, or causes it to be taken out, or approves of its being taken out—up to the point of enjoying it;

whichever monk takes out bulbs, roots, leaves, flowers, fruits, or seeds from his alms-bowl, or causes them to be taken out, or having had them taken out, accepts them when they are being offered, or approves of one who so accepts them.
Whichever monk extracts medicinal seeds from his alms-bowl, or [does so] up to the point of approving it;
whichever monk extracts mobile living beings from his alms-bowl, or [does so] up to the point of approving it;
whichever monk shakes his alms-bowl, causes it to be shaken, or approves of one who has shaken it being given to him when he accepts it or approves of another who accepts it.

Whichever monk, having repeatedly solicited a leader, a non-leader, a lay follower, or a non-follower—whether in the interior of a village or on the path between villages—causes them to give alms-bowl requisites, or approves of one who so causes them to give, commits an offense.

Whichever monk, having caused a leader, a non-leader, a lay follower, or a non-follower to rise from the midst of the assembly, repeatedly solicits them for alms-bowl requisites, or approves of one who so solicits them, commits an offense.
Whichever monk dwells during the rainy season depending upon an alms-bowl, or approves of one who so dwells, commits an offense.
Whatever monk dwells during the rainy season depending upon an alms-bowl,
or approves of one who so dwells— by indulging in that, he incurs a four-month period of penance (parihāra-ṭṭhāṇa) with suspension (ugghātiya).

Whichever monk speaks harshly to monks, or approves of one who speaks so; whichever monk speaks cruelly to monks, or approves of one who speaks so; whichever monk speaks both harshly and cruelly to monks, or approves of one who speaks so.
Whichever monk intimidates other monks with any form of intimidation, or approves of one who is intimidating;

whichever monk eats mangoes that still possess consciousness, or approves of one who is eating them; whichever monk spits on mangoes that still possess consciousness, or approves of one who is spitting on them.

Whichever monk eats mangoes with their skin on, or mango pulp, or mango peelings, or mango stalks, or mango seeds, or mango rind, or causes another to eat them, or approves of one who eats them; whichever monk spits out mangoes with their skin on, or [any of the aforementioned parts] up to the mango rind, or causes another to spit them out, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk eats mangoes placed upon something containing living beings, or causes another to eat them, or approves of one who does so.

Whichever monk chews or causes another to chew mango fruit placed upon a living plant, or approves of such an act; whichever monk eats or causes another to eat mango fruit placed upon a living plant, or approves of such an act; whichever monk chews or causes another to chew mango fruit placed upon a living plant, or approves of such an act.

Whichever monk causes a follower of another sect or a householder to massage or rub his own feet, or approves of one who is having them massaged or rubbed; whichever monk causes a follower of another sect or a householder to knead or rub his own feet, or approves of one who is having them kneaded or rubbed.

Whichever monk should cause his own feet to be anointed or smeared with oil, ghee, fat, or butter by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or should approve of [another] doing so; whichever monk should cause his own feet to be rubbed or scrubbed with lodhra, kakkola, powder, or cosmetic paste by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or should approve of [another] doing so.

Whichever monk causes his own feet to be washed, rinsed, or scrubbed by a member of another sect or a householder with cold water or warm water, or consents to another doing so; whichever monk causes his own feet to be blown upon or rubbed by a member of another sect or a householder, or consents to another doing so.

Whichever monk causes his own body to be rubbed or scrubbed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of [another] having it rubbed or scrubbed, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk causes his own body to be massaged or kneaded by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of [another] having it massaged or kneaded, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk causes his own body to be anointed or smeared with oil, ghee, fat, or butter by a member of another sect or a householder, or approves of one who is so anointing or smearing it;

whichever monk causes his own body to be rubbed or massaged with lodhra, karka, powder, or cosmetic paste by a member of another sect or a householder, or approves of one who is so rubbing or massaging it.

Whichever monk causes his own body to be splashed or washed with cold water or warm water by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or consents to another doing so; whichever monk causes his own body to be blown upon or rubbed dry by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or consents to another doing so.

Whichever monk causes a follower of another sect or a householder to rub or scrub a wound on his own body, or approves of one who is rubbing or scrubbing it; whichever monk causes a follower of another sect or a householder to massage or knead a wound on his own body, or approves of one who is massaging or kneading it.
Whichever monk causes a wound on his own body to be anointed or smeared with oil, ghee, fat, or butter by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or consents to such anointing or smearing;

whichever monk causes a wound on his own body to be rubbed or massaged with lodhra, kakkola, powder, or cosmetic paste by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or consents to such rubbing or massaging.

Whichever monk causes a wound on his own body to be rinsed or washed with cold water or warm water by a member of another sect or a householder, or consents to another doing so; whichever monk causes a wound on his own body to be fomented or dusted by a member of another sect or a householder, or consents to another doing so.

Whichever monk causes a tumor, a boil, an ulcer, a wound, or a fistula on his own body to be cut or lanced by another sectarian or a householder using any kind of sharp instrument—or consents to another who is doing so—is guilty of an offense.
Whichever monk, having had it cut or lanced, causes pus or blood to be extracted or cleansed by another sectarian or a householder—or consents to another who is doing so—is guilty of an offense.

Whichever monk, having had [himself] cleansed by a follower of another sect or [by anyone else up to] having had [himself] purified, has someone rinse him with cold water or warm water, or has someone wash him, or approves of one who is rinsing or washing him; whichever monk, having had [himself] washed by a follower of another sect or [by anyone else up to] having had [himself] washed, has someone smear him or rub him with any kind of ointment, or has someone smear or rub him, or approves of one who is smearing or rubbing him.

Whatever monk, having had [the body] washed by one belonging to another sect or [by others up to] having had it rinsed, or having had it smeared or plastered with any kind of ointment, or having had it anointed or rubbed with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or who approves of such anointing or rubbing—[commits an offense].

Any monk who, having had [the body] washed by one belonging to another sect, or having had it smeared or plastered with any kind of ointment, or having had it anointed or rubbed with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or having had it fumigated or perfumed with any kind of incense, or who approves of such an act—[commits an offense].

Whichever monk causes a member of another sect or a householder to extract, or causes someone else to extract, from his own finger any worm found therein, whether it be a worm in the nail or a worm in the flesh, or who approves of such an act; whichever monk has long nails trimmed or shaped by a member of another sect or a householder, or causes them to be so done, or approves of such an act.
Whichever monk causes a follower of another sect or a householder to trim or arrange his long leg-hairs, or approves of one who is trimming or arranging them;
whichever monk causes a follower of another sect or a householder to trim or arrange his long pubic hairs, or approves of one who is trimming or arranging them.

Whichever monk causes another sectarian or a householder to trim or arrange his own long eyelashes, or approves of another doing so; whichever monk causes another sectarian or a householder to trim or arrange his own long armpit hairs, or approves of another doing so.

Whichever monk causes his long body-hair or facial hair to be trimmed or shaped by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or consents to such trimming or shaping being done, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk causes his teeth to be rubbed or polished by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or consents to such rubbing or polishing being done, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk causes his own teeth to be rinsed or washed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or consents to [another] having them rinsed or washed; whichever monk causes his own teeth to be blown upon or polished by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or consents to [another] having them blown upon or polished; whichever monk causes his own thighs to be rubbed or massaged by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or consents to [another] having them rubbed or massaged.

Whichever monk causes his own limbs to be rubbed or massaged by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or consents to someone else rubbing or massaging them, commits an offense. Whichever monk causes his own limbs to be anointed or smeared with oil, ghee, fat, or butter by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or consents to someone else anointing or smearing them, commits an offense.

Whichever monk causes his own body to be rubbed with oil, or kneaded with lodhra, or scrubbed with paste, or anointed with color by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or consents to [another] rubbing it or kneading it—he commits an offense.

Whichever monk causes his own body to be rinsed with cold water or warm water by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or causes it to be washed, or consents to [another] rinsing it or washing it—he commits an offense.

Whichever monk causes his own beard to be shaved or dyed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of such shaving or dyeing, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk causes his own long upper-lip hairs to be trimmed or shaped by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of such trimming or shaping, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk causes his own long nose-hairs to be trimmed or arranged by a member of another sect or a householder, or approves of such trimming or arranging, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk causes his own long eyelashes to be trimmed or arranged by a member of another sect or a householder, or approves of such trimming or arranging, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk causes his own eyes to be rubbed or wiped by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or consents to [another] rubbing or wiping them, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk causes his own eyes to be massaged or kneaded by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or consents to [another] massaging or kneading them, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk causes his own eyes to be anointed with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or causes them to be smeared [with these], or approves of someone else causing them to be so anointed or smeared;

whichever monk causes his own eyes to be rubbed with lodhra, kakkola, powder, or cosmetic paste, or causes them to be massaged [with these], or approves of someone else causing them to be so rubbed or massaged.

Whichever monk causes his own eyes to be sprinkled or washed with cold water or warm water by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of such sprinkling or washing, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk causes his own eyes to be blown upon or dusted by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of such blowing upon or dusting, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk causes his own long eyebrow-hairs to be trimmed or shaped by a member of another sect or by a householder, or approves of one who is having them trimmed or shaped; whichever monk causes his own long arm-hairs to be trimmed or shaped by a member of another sect or by a householder, or approves of one who is having them trimmed or shaped.

Whichever monk causes a follower of another sect or a householder to remove or cleanse sweat, dirt, mud, or filth from his own body, or approves of one who is removing or cleansing it; whichever monk causes a follower of another sect or a householder to remove or cleanse the impurity of the eyes, the impurity of the ears, the impurity of the teeth, or the impurity of the nails from himself, or approves of one who is removing or cleansing it.
Whichever monk, while traveling from village to village with a follower of another sect or a householder, causes his own head-dress to be made, or approves of one who is having it made;
whichever monk disposes of excrement or urine in guest-houses, in park-houses, in the houses of householders, or in hermitages, or approves of one who is disposing of them.

Whichever monk disposes of feces or urine in a garden, or in a garden house, or in a garden hall; or in a street, or in a street house, or in a street hall—[or approves of one who so disposes of them]—he commits an offense.

Whichever monk disposes of feces or urine on a rampart, or on a watchtower, or on a wall, or on a parapet, or at a gate, or at a city-gate—[or approves of one who so disposes of them]—he commits an offense.
Whichever monk disposes of feces or urine on a watercourse, or on a path by water, or on a riverbank, or in a place where there is standing water, or approves of one who so disposes of them;

whichever monk disposes of feces or urine in an empty house, or in an empty hall, or in a ruined house, or in a ruined hall, or in a gabled building, or in a storehouse, or approves of one who so disposes of them.
Whichever monk disposes of feces or urine in a grass-hall, a grass-hut, a husk-hall, a husk-hut, a chaff-hall, or a chaff-hut—or approves of one who so disposes of them—is guilty of an offense.
Whichever monk disposes of feces or urine in a carriage-hall, a carriage-hut, a cart-hall, or a cart-hut—or approves of one who so disposes of them—is guilty of an offense.

Whichever monk consents to a monk depositing feces or urine in a shop, a shop-house, a market-hall, a market-house, a workshop, or a workshop-house—or whoever deposits them there—is guilty of an offense.
Whichever monk consents to a monk depositing feces or urine in a cow-stable, a cow-house, a great family’s residence, or a great house—or whoever deposits them there—is guilty of an offense.

Whichever monk gives food, drink, hard food, or soft food to one who is not a fellow-monk (ananyatīrthika) or to a householder, or approves of one giving it; or receives it, or approves of one receiving it. Whichever monk gives clothing, a bowl, a blanket, or a water-strainer to one who is not a fellow-monk or to a householder, or approves of one giving it; or receives it, or approves of one receiving it.

Whichever monk gives food, drink, soft food, or solid food to one who is living in association with the laity (pāsattha), or approves of one giving it—[he commits an offense]. Whichever monk receives food from one who is living in association with the laity, up to [receiving] solid food, or approves of one receiving it—[he commits an offense].
Whichever monk gives a robe, an alms-bowl, a blanket, or a foot-cloth to one who is living in association with the laity, or approves of one giving it—[he commits an offense].
Whichever monk accepts a robe or [any other requisite] from one who is living in association (*pāsattha*), or approves of one who so accepts it;

whichever monk gives food, drink, solid food, or delicacy to one who is lax (*ōsanna*), or approves of one who so gives it; whichever monk accepts food or [any other requisite] from one who is lax, or approves of one who so accepts it.
Whichever monk gives a robe, an alms-bowl, a blanket, or a water-strainer to one who is indolent, or approves of one giving them;

whichever monk receives a robe, or [any item] up to a water-strainer, from one who is indolent, or approves of one receiving them; whichever monk gives food, or [any item] up to a water-strainer, to one who is lazy, or approves of one giving it.
Whichever monk accepts food or [other requisites] from one who is indolent, or approves of another who is accepting them;

whichever monk gives clothing or [other requisites] to one who is indolent, or approves of another who is giving them; whichever monk accepts clothing or [other requisites] from one who is indolent, or approves of another who is accepting them.

Whichever monk gives food, or [anything up to] a dwelling, to a non-monastic, or approves of one who is giving it; whichever monk receives food, or [anything up to] a dwelling, from a non-monastic, or approves of one who is receiving it;
whichever monk gives clothing, or [anything up to] a dwelling, to a non-monastic, or approves of one who is giving it.
Whichever monk approves of a monk receiving a robe or [other requisites] from one who is habitually associated with householders, or approves of him while he is receiving them;

whichever monk approves of giving food, drink, solid food, or delicacy to one who is habitually associated with householders, or approves of him while he is giving them; whichever monk approves of receiving food or [other requisites] from one who is habitually associated with householders, or approves of him while he is receiving them.

Whichever monk gives clothing or [other requisites] to one who is in close association, or approves of one giving them, commits an offense. Whichever monk accepts clothing or [other requisites] from one who is in close association, or approves of one accepting them, commits an offense.

Whichever monk accepts clothing that has been requested, or clothing offered as an invitation, without having first ascertained, inquired about, or sought permission regarding it, or approves of one so accepting, commits an offense. Such clothing may be of four kinds: that which is constantly worn, that for bathing, that for festivals, or that for the royal gate.

Whichever monk, out of a desire for ornamentation, should rub or wipe his own feet, or should approve of one who is rubbing or wiping them; whichever monk, out of a desire for ornamentation, should massage or knead his own feet, or should approve of one who is massaging or kneading them; whichever monk, out of a desire for ornamentation, should anoint or smear his own feet with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or should approve of one who is anointing or smearing them.

Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, rubs or massages his own feet with lodhra, or with karka, or with powder, or with ointment, or approves of one who is rubbing or massaging them; whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, washes or rinses his own feet with cold water or warm water, or approves of one who is washing or rinsing them;
whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, fans or colors his own feet, or approves of one who is fanning or coloring them.

Whichever monk, out of a desire for ornamentation, should rub or wipe his own body, or should approve of one who is rubbing or wiping it; whichever monk, out of a desire for ornamentation, should massage or knead his own body, or should approve of one who is massaging or kneading it; whichever monk, out of a desire for ornamentation, should anoint or smear his own body with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or should approve of one who is anointing or smearing it.

Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, rubs or smears his own body with lodhra, or with kakkola, or with powder, or with cosmetic paste, or approves of one who is rubbing or smearing it; whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, washes or rinses his own body with cold water or warm water, or approves of one who is washing or rinsing it; whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, fans or colors his own body, or approves of one who is fanning or coloring it.

Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, rubs or cleanses a wound on his own body, or approves of one who is rubbing or cleansing it, commits an offense. Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, massages or rubs a wound on his own body, or approves of one who is massaging or rubbing it, commits an offense. Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, anoints or smears a wound on his own body with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or approves of one who is anointing or smearing it, commits an offense.

Whichever monk, out of a desire for ornamentation, should rub or scrub a wound on his own body with lodhra, or with karka, or with powder, or with ointment—whether he does so himself or approves of another doing so.
Whichever monk, out of a desire for ornamentation, should wash or rinse a wound on his own body with cold water or warm water—whether he does so himself or approves of another doing so.
Whichever monk, out of a desire for ornamentation, should fumigate or color his own body, or should approve of one who is fumigating or coloring it;

whichever monk, out of a desire for ornamentation, should with any kind of sharp instrument cut or lacerate a boil, a carbuncle, an ulcer, a fissure, or a fistula on his own body, or should approve of one who is cutting or lacerating it.

Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should extract pus or blood from a boil or [other growth] on his own body—whether he himself extracts it or cleanses it, or approves of one who extracts it or cleanses it—[commits an offense]. Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should wash or rinse with cold water or warm water a boil or [other growth] on his own body—whether he himself washes or rinses it, or approves of one who washes or rinses it—[commits an offense].

Whatever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should wash or bathe a boil or [other ailment] on his own body, or should smear or anoint it with any kind of ointment, or should approve of one who is so smearing or anointing it, [commits an offense].

Whatever monk, out of a desire for ornamentation, having washed his own body from head to foot, or having smeared or anointed it with any kind of ointment, or having massaged or rubbed it with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or who approves of another doing so, commits an offense.

Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, having anointed or smeared his own body with ghee or even with butter, or having fumigated or re-fumigated it with any kind of incense, or approves of one who is so doing;
whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, repeatedly inserts and then extracts worms from his own nostrils or worms from his own ears, or approves of one who is so doing.

Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should trim or arrange his own long fingernails, or should approve of another doing so; whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should trim or arrange his own long leg-hairs, or should approve of another doing so;
whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should trim or arrange his own long pubic hairs, or should approve of another doing so.
Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should pluck or arrange his own long eyelashes, or should approve of one who plucks or arranges them;
whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should pluck or arrange the long hairs of his armpits, or should approve of one who plucks or arranges them;
whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should pluck or arrange the long hairs of his beard, or should approve of one who plucks or arranges them.
Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, rubs or polishes his own teeth, or approves of one who is rubbing or polishing them, commits an offense.
Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, rinses or washes his own teeth, or approves of one who is rinsing or washing them, commits an offense.
Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, blows on or colors his own teeth, or approves of one who is blowing on or coloring them, commits an offense.

Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should rub or stroke his own thighs, or should approve of one who is rubbing or stroking them; whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should massage or knead his own thighs, or should approve of one who is massaging or kneading them; whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should anoint or smear his own thighs with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or should approve of one who is anointing or smearing them.

Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, rubs or massages his own body with lodhra, kakkola, powder, or cosmetic paste—or approves of one who is rubbing or massaging it—is guilty of an offense. Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, washes or rinses his own body with cold water or warm water—or approves of one who is washing or rinsing it—is guilty of an offense. Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, fans or colors his own body—or approves of one who is fanning or coloring it—is guilty of an offense.
Whichever monk, out of a desire for ornamentation, should pluck or arrange the hairs on his upper lip, or should approve of another doing so;

whichever monk, out of a desire for ornamentation, should pluck or arrange his long nose-hairs, or should approve of another doing so; whichever monk, out of a desire for ornamentation, should pluck or arrange his long eyelashes, or should approve of another doing so.

Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should rub or wipe his own eyes, or should approve of one who is rubbing or wiping them; whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should massage or rub his own eyes, or should approve of one who is massaging or rubbing them; whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should anoint or smear his own eyes with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or should approve of one who is anointing or smearing them.

Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, rubs or smears his own eyes with lodhra, or with karka, or with powder, or with pigment—whether he does so himself or approves of one who does so; whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, washes or rinses his own eyes with cold water or warm water—whether he does so himself or approves of one who does so; whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, fans or colors his own eyes—whether he does so himself or approves of one who does so.

Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should pluck or arrange his own long eyebrow-hairs, or should approve of one who plucks or arranges them; whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should pluck or arrange his own long body-hairs on the sides, or should approve of one who plucks or arranges them; whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should remove or cleanse sweat, grime, mud, or dirt from his own body, or should approve of one who removes or cleanses it.
Whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should remove or clean his own eye-secretion, ear-secretion, tooth-secretion, or nail-secretion, or should approve of one who removes or cleans them;
whichever monk, while traveling from village to village out of a desire for adornment, should have a head-covering made for himself, or should approve of one who has it made;
whichever monk, out of a desire for adornment, should wear a cloth, a bowl, a blanket, a foot-wiper, or any other kind of accessory, or should approve of one who wears them.
Whatever monk, out of a desire for adornment, washes a robe, a bowl, a blanket, a foot-wiping cloth, or any other kind of accessory, or causes it to be washed,
incurs an offense of four months' duration that must be confessed. If he persists in such conduct,
he commits an offense requiring a four-month period of penance.
Whichever monk approaches a lodging belonging to a householder, or approves of one who is approaching it;
whichever monk enters a lodging containing water, or approves of one who is entering it;
whichever monk enters a lodging containing fire, or approves of one who is entering it.
Whichever monk eats sugarcane that still contains its own sap, or approves of one who so eats; whichever monk chews sugarcane that still contains its own sap, or approves of one who so chews;

whichever monk eats sugarcane that is still within its sheath, or sugarcane stalks, or sugarcane juice, or sugarcane syrup, or sugarcane shoots, or sugarcane sprouts—that is, sugarcane that still contains its own sap—or approves of one who so eats.

Whichever monk splits, or approves of another splitting, sugar-cane with living parts—whether it be a stalk of sugar-cane, a piece of sugar-cane, sugar-cane juice, sugar-cane molasses, a sugar-cane shed, or a sugar-cane field; or whichever monk eats sugar-cane placed upon living matter, or approves of another eating it;
or whichever monk splits sugar-cane placed upon living matter, or approves of another splitting it.

Whichever monk eats, or approves of another eating, sugar-cane juice, sugar-cane pieces, sugar-cane syrup, sugar-cane molasses, sugar-cane stalks, or sugar-cane dregs that have been placed in a vessel containing living beings;

or whichever monk chews, or approves of another chewing, sugar-cane juice, sugar-cane pieces, sugar-cane syrup, sugar-cane molasses, sugar-cane stalks, or sugar-cane dregs that have been placed in a vessel containing living beings.
Whichever monk accepts, or approves of another’s accepting, food, drink, solid food, or delicacy from forest-dwelling monks who have set out on a journey through the wilderness;
