whichever monk says that one who is not pure is pure, or approves of one who says so; whichever monk says that one who is pure is not pure, or approves of one who says so.

Whichever monk transfers from a community that has reached its goal (*vusirāta*) to a community that has not reached its goal (*avuṣirāta*), or approves of one who is so transferring, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk gives food, drink, soft food, or solid food to those who have entered into a dispute, or approves of one who is giving it, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk receives food, or even solid food, from those who have entered into a dispute, or approves of one who is receiving it, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk gives, or approves of another giving, a robe, an alms-bowl, a blanket, or a foot-wiping cloth to those who have entered into a conflict;

whichever monk receives, or approves of another receiving, a robe or anything up to a foot-wiping cloth from those who have entered into a conflict; whichever monk gives, or approves of another giving, a dwelling to those who have entered into a conflict.

Whichever monk accepts lodgings for those who have entered upon a conflict, or approves of one who so accepts them; whichever monk enters the lodgings of those who have entered upon a conflict, or approves of one who so enters; whichever monk gives instruction in the recitation of the scriptures to those who have entered upon a conflict, or approves of one who so gives it.
Whichever monk receives private instruction from those involved in a dispute, or approves of one who is receiving it;

whichever monk, when there are favorable conditions for wandering and people are settled in the countryside, intends to wander for the sake of residence in a forest that is difficult to traverse and lacks a path, or approves of one who so intends;

whichever monk, when there are favorable conditions for wandering and people are settled in the countryside, intends to wander for the sake of residence among various kinds of barbarian, ignoble, foreign, and border-dwelling tribes, or approves of one who so intends.
Whichever monk accepts food—or anything up to [the eight requisites]—in families that are held in contempt, or approves of one who so accepts it;
whichever monk accepts a robe—or anything up to [the eight requisites]—in families that are held in contempt, or approves of one who so accepts it;
whichever monk accepts a dwelling in families that are held in contempt, or approves of one who so accepts it.

Whichever monk recites the sacred texts (*sajjhāya*) in families that are held in contempt, or approves of one who is so reciting; whichever monk causes the sacred texts to be recited in families that are held in contempt, or approves of one who is so causing them to be recited; whichever monk receives the sacred texts in families that are held in contempt, or approves of one who is so receiving them.

Whichever monk places food, or [any of the other requisites] up to a seat, upon the earth, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk places food, or [any of the other requisites] up to a bed, upon the ground, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk places food, drink, solid food, or delicacy in the air, or approves of one who does so.

Whichever monk eats together with those of other sects or householders, or approves of one who so eats; whichever monk eats while being surrounded or encircled by those of other sects or householders, or approves of one who so eats; whichever monk, having touched the bedding or mat of his preceptors or teachers with his foot, goes away without first obtaining permission with his hand, or approves of one who so goes.
Whichever monk wears an outfit that exceeds the prescribed measure in size or number, or approves of another wearing one, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk disposes of excrement or urine on bare ground, or approves of another disposing of it, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk disposes of excrement or urine on moist ground, or approves of another doing so, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk consents to voiding excrement or urine on earth covered with living organisms; whichever monk consents to voiding excrement or urine on unbaked clay earth;
whichever monk deposits excrement or urine on earth containing living beings, or consents to one who is so depositing it.

Whichever monk disposes of excrement or urine on a stone containing living beings, or approves of one who so disposes of it, [commits an offense]. Whichever monk disposes of excrement or urine on a mound containing living beings, or approves of one who so disposes of it, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk consents to disposing of excrement or urine upon a termite-hill, or upon wood inhabited by living beings, containing eggs, containing creatures, containing seeds, containing sprouts, containing moisture, or covered with ant-hills, moss, water-lichen, mud, or spiderwebs, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk disposes of feces or urine upon a pillar, a house-rafter, a peg, a water-channel, or any other such thing growing out of the open space—whether it be poorly fastened, poorly placed, unstable, or shaky—and whoever approves of one who so disposes of them, commits an offense. Whichever monk disposes of feces or urine upon a wooden beam, a wall, a stone, a brick, or any other such thing—as far as [the previous description]—and whoever approves of one who so disposes of them, commits an offense.
Whatever monk disposes of feces or urine on a pillar, a threshold, a bed, a pavilion, a gallery, a palace, the ground floor, or any other such place—
whether he himself disposes of it or consents to another doing so— he, by practicing that, incurs a four-month penance involving forfeiture.

Whichever monk, out of curiosity, binds any kind of living creature belonging to the class of mobile beings with a grass noose, a muñja-grass noose, a wooden noose, a leather noose, a cane noose, a rope noose, or a thread noose, or approves of one who is binding them; whichever monk, out of curiosity, releases any kind of living creature belonging to the class of mobile beings that has been bound with a grass noose, or even a rope noose, or a thread noose, or approves of one who is releasing it.

Whichever monk, out of a desire for amusement, makes a garland of grass, or a garland of *mujja* reeds, or a garland of cane, or a garland of *bhiṇḍa* seeds, or a garland of *madana* seeds, or a garland of feathers, or a garland of ivory, or a garland of horn, or a garland of conch-shell, or a garland of bone, or a garland of wood, or a garland of leaves, or a garland of flowers, or a garland of fruit, or a garland of seeds, or a garland of green plants, or causes one to make them, or approves of one who does so.
Whichever monk, out of curiosity, wears a garland of grass, or even a garland of green herbs, or approves of one who wears them;
whichever monk, out of curiosity, wears a garland of grass, or even a garland of green herbs, or approves of one who wears them.
Whichever monk, out of curiosity, fashions objects of iron, or copper, or bronze, or lead, or silver, or gold, or approves of one who fashions them.
Whichever monk, out of curiosity, keeps iron, copper, tin, lead, silver, or gold, or approves of one who keeps them;
whichever monk, out of curiosity, uses iron, copper, tin, lead, silver, or gold, or approves of one who uses them.

Whichever monk, out of curiosity, has necklaces or half-necklaces, single-strand necklaces, pearl necklaces, gold necklaces, gemstone necklaces, bracelets, armlets, bangles, earrings, turbans, crowns, or hanging threads, or golden threads made, or causes them to be made, or approves of their being made;
whichever monk, out of curiosity, wears necklaces or half-necklaces, up to crowns, or hanging threads, or golden threads, or causes them to be worn, or approves of their being worn.
Whichever monk, out of curiosity, ties on necklaces, or half-necklaces, or even crowns, or long strings, or gold threads, or causes them to be tied on, or approves of their being tied on.

Whichever monk, out of curiosity, has made, or causes to be made, or approves of the making of—fine woolens (*āīṇa*), or fine cotton cloths (*sahiṇa*), or auspicious cloths (*kallāṇa*), or fine auspicious cloths (*sahiṇakallāṇa*), or *āya* cloth, or *kāya* cloth, or *khoma* cloth, or *dugulla* cloth, or *tirīḍapaṭṭa* cloth, or *malaya* cloth, or *pattuṇṇa* cloth, or *aṃsuya* cloth, or *cīṇaṃsuya* cloth, or *dēsarāgaṇa* cloth, or *amilāṇa* cloth, or *gajjalāṇa* cloth, or *phāḍiyāga* cloth, or *kōtavāṇa* cloth, or blankets (*kambala*), or *pāvāraga* cloaks, or gold-colored cloths, or cloths worked with gold threads (*kanagakatāṇa*), or cloths with gold patterns (*kanagapaṭṭa*), or cloths inlaid with gold (*kanagakhaciya*), or cloths embroidered with gold flowers (*kanagaphulli*), or tiger-skin cloths, or cloths resembling tiger-skin, or ornaments, or cloths variegated with ornaments, or *udda* skins, or skins of the *goramiga* deer, or skins of the black deer, or skins of the blue deer, or *pēsa* skins, or skins variegated with *pēsa*—he commits an offense.

Whichever monk, out of curiosity, wears—or approves of another wearing—woolen cloths (*āīṇa*) or, up to and including, cloths made from the hair of the blue deer (*nīlamiga*), whether they be woven or unwoven;
whichever monk, out of curiosity, uses—or approves of another using—woolen cloths or, up to and including, cloths made from the hair of the blue deer, whether they be woven or unwoven.
Whichever nun approves of a nun having her feet massaged or rubbed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of such massaging or rubbing being done.
Any nun who has a naked mendicant’s feet massaged or rubbed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or who approves of such massaging or rubbing being done, [commits an offense].

Any nun who has a naked mendicant’s feet anointed or smeared with oil, ghee, fat, or butter by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or who approves of such anointing or smearing being done, [commits an offense].
Any nun who has another sectarian or a householder massage or rub the feet of a naked mendicant with oil, ointment, powder, or dye, or who approves of another doing so;
any nun who has another sectarian or a householder rinse or wash the feet of a naked mendicant with cold water or warm water, or who approves of another doing so.

Any nun who has another sectarian or a householder blow on or polish the feet of a naked mendicant, or who approves of another doing so, commits an offense. Any nun who has another sectarian or a householder massage or rub the body of a naked mendicant, or who approves of another doing so, commits an offense.

Whichever nun causes a naked mendicant’s body to be massaged or rubbed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of such massaging or rubbing being done, [commits an offense]. Whichever nun causes a naked mendicant’s body to be anointed or smeared with oil, ghee, fat, or butter by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of such anointing or smearing being done, [commits an offense].

Whichever nun causes a naked mendicant’s body to be rubbed with lodhra, karka, powder, or cosmetic by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or causes it to be massaged, or approves of such rubbing or massaging; whichever nun causes a naked mendicant’s body to be rinsed or washed with cold water or warm water by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or causes it to be rinsed or washed, or approves of such rinsing or washing.

Whichever nun causes a naked mendicant’s body to be blown upon or smeared with [ointment] by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of such an act being done, [commits an offense]. Whichever nun causes a wound on a naked mendicant’s body to be rubbed or wiped by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of such an act being done, [commits an offense].

Any nun who has a wound on her body massaged or rubbed by a member of another sect or a householder, or who consents to [another] having it massaged or rubbed; any nun who has a wound on her body anointed or smeared with oil, ghee, fat, or butter by a member of another sect or a householder, or who consents to [another] having it anointed or smeared.

Any nun who has a wound on the body of a naked mendicant (nirgrantha) rubbed with lodhra, karka, powder, or pigment by a member of another sect or a householder, or has it massaged, or approves of one who is rubbing or massaging it;

or any nun who has a wound on the body of a naked mendicant rinsed or washed with cold water or warm water by a member of another sect or a householder, or has it rinsed or washed, or approves of one who is rinsing or washing it.

Any nun who causes a wound on the body of a *nirgrantha* to be blown upon or smeared with [medicinal paste] by a member of another sect or a householder, or who approves of one doing so, commits an offense.

Any nun who causes a boil, a carbuncle, an ulcer, a fissure, or a fistula on the body of a *nirgrantha* to be cut or incised by a member of another sect or a householder using any kind of sharp instrument, or who approves of one doing so, commits an offense.

Whichever nun causes a boil or a carbuncle on the body of a naked mendicant (nirgrantha)—up to the point of having it cut out or having it lanced, or having the pus or blood extracted or cleansed, or causing another to extract or cleanse it—is at fault.

Whichever nun, having had a boil or [other ailment] on the body of a naked mendicant extracted or cleansed, causes it to be sprinkled or washed with cold water or warm water, or causes another to sprinkle or wash it—is at fault.

Any nun who, having had a boil or [other ailment] on the body of a naked mendicant lanced, or even having had it washed, has it smeared or plastered with any kind of ointment, or approves of one who is so smearing or plastering it; or any nun who, having had a boil or [other ailment] on the body of a naked mendicant lanced, or even having had it washed, or having had it smeared or plastered, has it anointed or rubbed with oil, ghee, fat, or butter, or approves of one who is so anointing or rubbing it.

Any nun who, having had a boil or [other ailment] on the body of a naked mendicant (nirgrantha) anointed or massaged, causes it to be fumigated or re-fumigated with any kind of incense, or consents to another doing so;

or any nun who, by means of her finger, has a worm from the nails or a worm from the belly of a naked mendicant inserted and then extracted by a member of another sect or a householder, or consents to another doing so.

Whichever nun causes the long nails of a naked ascetic (nirgrantha) to be trimmed or shaped by a member of another sect or by a householder, or approves of their being trimmed or shaped—[she commits an offense]. Whichever nun causes the long hair on the shanks of a naked ascetic to be trimmed or shaped by a member of another sect or by a householder, or approves of their being trimmed or shaped—[she commits an offense].

Whichever nun causes the long pubic hairs of a naked mendicant (nirgrantha) to be trimmed or arranged by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of their being trimmed or arranged—[she incurs an offense]. Whichever nun causes the long eyelashes of a naked mendicant to be trimmed or arranged by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of their being trimmed or arranged—[she incurs an offense].
Any nun who has another sectarian or a householder shave or trim the long hair of the armpits of a naked mendicant, or approves of another doing so;
or any nun who has another sectarian or a householder shave or trim the long hair of the pubic region of a naked mendicant, or approves of another doing so.

Any nun who has another sectarian or a householder rub or scrub the teeth of a naked mendicant, or consents to another doing so, commits an offense. Any nun who has another sectarian or a householder rinse or wash the teeth of a naked mendicant, or consents to another doing so, commits an offense.

Any nun who has a tooth-stick for a monk cleaned or dyed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or who approves of its being cleaned or dyed; or any nun who has a tooth-stick for a monk massaged or wiped by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or who approves of its being massaged or wiped.

Any nun who, for the sake of a naked ascetic (nirgrantha), has herself massaged or rubbed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or consents to another being so massaged or rubbed; any nun who, for the sake of a naked ascetic, has herself anointed or smeared with oil, ghee, fat, or butter by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or consents to another being so anointed or smeared.

Any nun who, for the sake of a naked ascetic (nirgrantha), has him rubbed or massaged on the body by one belonging to another sect, a householder, or by means of lodhra, kakka, powder, or cosmetic paste—whether she herself causes it to be done or approves of its being done; any nun who, for the sake of a naked ascetic, has him rinsed or washed on the body with cold water or warm water by one belonging to another sect or a householder—whether she herself causes it to be done or approves of its being done.

If a nun causes a naked mendicant to have his hair or beard combed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or causes him to have it dyed, or consents to his having it combed or dyed, she commits an offense.

If a nun causes the long upper-lip hair of a monk to be trimmed or shaped by a member of another sect or by a householder, or if she approves of another doing so; [if a nun causes the long nose-hair of a monk to be trimmed or shaped by a member of another sect or by a householder, or if she approves of another doing so].

Any nun who has another sectarian or a householder trim or shape the long eyelashes of a naked mendicant, or consents to another doing so; or any nun who has another sectarian or a householder massage or rub the eyes of a naked mendicant, or consents to another doing so.

Whichever nun should have a naked mendicant’s eyes massaged or rubbed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or should approve of such massaging or rubbing being done—[she incurs an offense].

Whichever nun should have a naked mendicant’s eyes anointed or smeared with oil, ghee, fat, or butter by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or should approve of such anointing or smearing being done—[she incurs an offense].

Any nun who has a naked mendicant’s eyes rubbed or massaged with lodhra, karka, powder, or pigment by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or who approves of such rubbing or massaging, [commits an offense]. Any nun who has a naked mendicant’s eyes sprinkled or washed with cold water or warm water by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or who approves of such sprinkling or washing, [commits an offense].

Any nun who causes the eyes of a naked mendicant to be cleansed or anointed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or who consents to another doing so; or any nun who causes the long hairs on the eyebrows of a naked mendicant to be trimmed or shaped by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or who consents to another doing so.

Any nun who has another sectarian or a householder trim or arrange the long hair on the body of a naked mendicant, or consents to another’s doing so; or any nun who has another sectarian or a householder remove or cleanse sweat, grime, mud, or dirt from the body of a naked mendicant, or consents to another’s doing so.
Any nun who causes a naked mendicant to have the impurity of her eyes, ears, teeth, or nails removed by a member of another sect or a householder, or who consents to one doing so, commits an offense.

Any nun who causes a naked mendicant, while traveling from village to village, to have his head shaved by a member of another sect or a householder, or who consents to one doing so, commits an offense.
Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her feet massaged or rubbed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of [another] having them massaged or rubbed;
whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her feet rubbed or kneaded by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of [another] having them rubbed or kneaded.

Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her feet massaged or rubbed with oil, ghee, fat, or butter by a member of another sect or a householder, or [of one who is] having them massaged or rubbed—[he incurs a fault].

Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her feet scrubbed or rubbed with lodhra, kakkola, powder, or cosmetic paste by a member of another sect or a householder, or [of one who is] having them scrubbed or rubbed—[he incurs a fault].

Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her feet scrubbed or washed by a member of another sect or a householder with cold water or warm water—whether he himself performs the scrubbing or washing, or causes another to do so—he commits an offense. Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her feet blown upon or dusted by a member of another sect or a householder—whether he himself performs the blowing or dusting, or causes another to do so—he commits an offense.
Whichever Nirgrantha approves when a Nirgranthī has her body massaged or rubbed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves while she is having it massaged or rubbed;
whichever Nirgrantha approves when a Nirgranthī has her body rubbed with oil or kneaded by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves while she is having it rubbed or kneaded.

Whosoever among the *nirgranthas* approves of a *nirgranthī* having her body massaged or rubbed with oil, ghee, fat, or butter by one belonging to another sect or by a householder—whether he himself causes it to be done or approves of its being done.

Whosoever among the *nirgranthas* approves of a *nirgranthī* having her body rubbed with lodhra-paste, kakkola-paste, powder, or cosmetic ointment by one belonging to another sect or by a householder—whether he himself causes it to be done or approves of its being done.

Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her feet scrubbed or washed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, using either cold water or warm water; or whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her body fanned or dusted by one belonging to another sect or by a householder—[he incurs a fault].
Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her body massaged or rubbed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or [himself] having it massaged or rubbed;
whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her body massaged or rubbed with oil or kneaded by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or [himself] having it massaged or kneaded.

If a Nirgrantha [monk] causes a wound on the body of a Nirgranthī [nun] to be massaged or smeared with oil, ghee, fat, or butter by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or if he approves of such massaging or smearing being done—[he incurs a fault].

If a Nirgrantha causes a wound on the body of a Nirgranthī to be washed or rubbed with lodhra, kakkola, powder, or cosmetic paste by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or if he approves of such washing or rubbing being done—[he incurs a fault].
Whichever Nirgrantha approves when another Nirgrantha’s wound on the body is being rinsed or washed with cold water or warm water by one belonging to another sect or by a householder;
or whichever Nirgrantha approves when another Nirgrantha’s wound on the body is being fomented or dusted with powder by one belonging to another sect or by a householder.

If a Nirgrantha causes a Nirgranthī to have a boil, a carbuncle, a sore, a wound, or a fistula on her body lanced, incised, or cut by another belonging to a different sect or by a householder, using any kind of sharp instrument—whether he himself performs the lancing or incising, or causes another to do so, or consents to another’s lancing or incising—it is an offense.

Whichever *nirgrantha* should have a boil or [other ailment] on the body of a *nirgranthī*, up to the point of being caused by a weapon, have it cut away or have it lanced, or have pus or blood removed, or have it cleansed; or [should he] cause it to be removed or cleansed—[he commits a *sātisāra* offense].

Whichever *nirgrantha* should, after having had a boil or [other ailment] on the body of a *nirgranthī* removed or cleansed, have it sprinkled or washed with cold water or warm water; or [should he] cause it to be sprinkled or washed—[he commits a *sātisāra* offense].

Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having a boil or [other ailment] on her body being rubbed or washed, or having it smeared or plastered with any kind of ointment— whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having a boil or [other ailment] on her body being anointed or rubbed with oil, ghee, fat, or butter— [commits an offense].
Whichever monk, having had a boil or [other ailment] on the body of a nun massaged or rubbed with oil, or having had it cleansed or thoroughly cleansed with any kind of ointment, approves of it.

Whichever monk, having had an intestinal worm or a vaginal worm removed from a nun by a member of another sect or a householder, having had it inserted finger-deep again and again, or having had it extracted, approves of it.

Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her long nails trimmed or shaped by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or of her having them being trimmed or shaped—[he incurs a fault]. Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having the long hair on her calves trimmed or shaped by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or of her having it being trimmed or shaped—[he incurs a fault].

Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having the long hairs of her pubic region trimmed or shaped by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of someone else having them trimmed or shaped;

whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having the long eyelashes trimmed or shaped by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of someone else having them trimmed or shaped.

Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having the long hair of her armpits trimmed or shaped by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of someone else having it trimmed or shaped;

whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having the long hair of her private parts trimmed or shaped by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of someone else having it trimmed or shaped.

Whosoever among the *nirgranthas* consents to a *nirgranthī* whose teeth have been rubbed or scrubbed by a follower of another sect or by a householder, or causes them to be rubbed or scrubbed; whosoever among the *nirgranthas* consents to a *nirgranthī* whose teeth have been rinsed or washed by a follower of another sect or by a householder, or causes them to be rinsed or washed.
Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her teeth cleaned or dyed by a member of another sect or by a householder, or [himself] cleaning or dyeing them;
whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her lips massaged or rubbed by a member of another sect or by a householder, or [himself] massaging or rubbing them.

Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her limbs massaged or rubbed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or of her having them massaged or rubbed [by such a person], commits an offense.

Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her limbs anointed or smeared with oil, ghee, fat, or butter by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or of her having them anointed or smeared [by such a person], commits an offense.

Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her limbs rubbed or massaged by one belonging to another sect, or by a householder, using lodhra, karka, powder, or cosmetic paste—whether he himself causes them to be rubbed or massaged, or approves of someone else doing so.

Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her limbs rinsed or washed with cold water or warm water by one belonging to another sect, or by a householder—whether he himself causes them to be rinsed or washed, or approves of someone else doing so.

Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her lips blown-dried or dyed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or of that act being done, he commits an offense. Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having the long hairs on her upper lip trimmed or shaped by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or of that act being done, he commits an offense.

Whichever Nirgrantha or Nirgranthī causes long nose-hairs of another Nirgranthī to be trimmed or shaped by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of their being trimmed or shaped, commits an offense.

Whichever Nirgrantha or Nirgranthī causes long eyelashes of another Nirgranthī to be trimmed or shaped by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of their being trimmed or shaped, commits an offense.
Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her eyes massaged or rubbed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of [another] having them massaged or rubbed;

whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her eyes rubbed with oil or kneaded by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of [another] having them rubbed with oil or kneaded.

Whichever Nirgrantha approves when a Nirgranthī has her eyes massaged or rubbed with oil, ghee, fat, or butter by a member of another sect or a householder—or approves of someone else having them massaged or rubbed—[he incurs a fault].

Whichever Nirgrantha approves when a Nirgranthī has her eyes washed or cleansed with lodhra, karka, powder, or pigment by a member of another sect or a householder—or approves of someone else having them washed or cleansed—[he incurs a fault].

Whichever Nirgrantha [monk] has a Nirgranthī [nun] have her eyes washed or rinsed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, using either cold water or warm water—whether he himself causes them to wash or rinse them, or consents to another who is causing them to wash or rinse them—he incurs a *sātisāra* offense.

Whichever Nirgrantha [monk] has a Nirgranthī [nun] have her eyes blown upon or dusted by one belonging to another sect or by a householder—whether he himself causes them to blow upon or dust them, or consents to another who is causing them to blow upon or dust them—he incurs a *sātisāra* offense.

Whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having her long eyebrow-hairs trimmed or shaped by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of someone else trimming or shaping them;

whichever Nirgrantha approves of a Nirgranthī having the long hair on her sides trimmed or shaped by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or approves of someone else trimming or shaping it.

Whichever Nirgrantha causes a Nirgranthī to have sweat, or dirt, or mud, or filth removed from her body by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or causes it to be cleansed, or approves of one who is having it removed or cleansed—[he incurs a fault]. Whichever Nirgrantha causes a Nirgranthī to have the impurity of the eyes, or the impurity of the ears, or the impurity of the teeth, or the impurity of the nails removed by one belonging to another sect or by a householder, or causes it to be cleansed, or approves of one who is having it removed or cleansed—[he incurs a fault].

Whichever *nirgrantha* monk approves of another *nirgrantha* monk, or a householder, or one belonging to another sect, having his head shaved while a female *nirgrantha* is traveling from village to village;

or whichever *nirgrantha* monk, when there is space available within the vicinity of a fellow *nirgrantha*, does not give him space, or approves of one who does not give it; or whichever *nirgrantha* monk, when there is space available within the vicinity of a fellow female *nirgrantha*, does not give her space, or approves of one who does not give it.
Whichever monk accepts food, drink, soft food, or solid food that has been brought from a garland-maker’s shop while it is being given, or approves of one who so accepts it;

whichever monk accepts food, drink, soft food, or solid food that has been taken from a storehouse by turning it upside down, overturning it, or drawing it out while it is being given, or approves of one who so accepts it;
whichever monk accepts food, drink, soft food, or solid food that has been scraped from a clay-smeared vessel while it is being given, or approves of one who so accepts it.
Whichever monk accepts food or [other requisites] resting upon the earth, or approves of one who so accepts;
whichever monk accepts food or [other requisites] resting upon water, or approves of one who so accepts;
whichever monk accepts food or [other requisites] resting upon fire, or approves of one who so accepts.
Whichever monk accepts food or drink established upon a body of vegetation, or one who is so accepting, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk, having blown upon or fanned with a winnowing basket, a fan, a palm-leaf fan, a leaf, a branch, a twig, a peacock-feather fan, a hand-fan made of peacock feathers, a cloth, the hem of a garment, or with his hand or mouth, accepts food or drink that has been brought and offered to him, or one who is so accepting, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk accepts, or approves of another’s accepting, fermented rice-gruel, fermented broth, rice-water, bean-soup water, sesame-water, husk-water, scum of boiled rice, sour gruel, sour sorrel, pure water, or fresh water that has not been washed, which is not sour, not yet settled, not fully digested, and not rendered harmless—[he commits an offense].
Whichever monk explains, or approves of another’s explaining, bodily marks for his own sake as being those of an Ācārya—[he commits an offense].

Whatever monk should sing, or laugh, or talk, or dance, or act out gestures; or should make the neighing of a horse, or the trumpeting of an elephant, or the shouts and lion-roars of battle—whether he does so himself or approves of another doing so.

Whatever monk intentionally listens to, or approves of another listening to, the sounds of kettledrums, or the sounds of small drums, or the sounds of clay drums, or the sounds of cymbals, or the sounds of the *nandi* drum, or the sounds of the *jhallari* drum, or the sounds of the *ḍamaruka* drum, or the sounds of the *maḍḍaya* drum, or the sounds of the *saduya* drum, or the sounds of the *pāesa* drum, or the sounds of the *gōluki* drum, or any other such sounds of stretched membranes for the purpose of hearing them with his ears—he commits an offense.

Whatever monk intentionally listens to, or approves of another listening to, the sounds of lutes, or the sounds of the *vipañci*, or the sounds of the *tuṇa*, or the sounds of the *baddhīsaga*, or the sounds of the *paṇava*, or the sounds of the *tumbavīṇā*, or the sounds of the *jhōḍaya*, or the sounds of the *ḍhaṅkuṇa*, or any other such sounds produced by strings, for the sake of hearing with his own ears—he commits an offense.

Whatever monk intentionally listens to the sounds of clapping hands, or the sounds of bronze cymbals, or the sounds of *lattiyā* drums, or the sounds of *gōhiya* drums, or the sounds of *makariya* drums, or the sounds of *kacchabhi* drums, or the sounds of *mahati* drums, or the sounds of *saṇāliya* drums, or the sounds of *vāliya* drums, or any other such solid (percussive) sounds for the sake of his ear-faculty, or approves of one who so listens—he commits an offense.

Whatever monk intentionally attends to, or approves of another who intentionally attends to, the sounds of conchs, or the sounds of flutes, or the sounds of reed-pipes, or the sounds of lutes, or the sounds of cymbals, or the sounds of drums, or any other such hollow-sounding noises with the purpose of listening through the ear—[he commits an offense].

Whatever monk, for the purpose of ear-ornamentation, gazes intently at cultivated fields, or embankments, or lotus ponds, or marshes, or waterfalls, or mountain torrents, or tanks, or lotus pools, or oblong ponds, or canals, or lakes, or rows of lakes, or series of lakes, or gazes intently [at them], or approves of one who so gazes—[this is an offense].
Whichever monk intentionally directs his hearing toward thickets, dense forests, wooded areas, groves, forest thickets, mountains, or mountain thickets for the sake of listening to sounds;

or whichever monk intentionally directs his hearing toward villages, towns, hamlets, market towns, fortified towns, seaports, cities, mines, caravan halting places, or settlements for the sake of listening to sounds—and whoever approves of such a monk [is guilty].

Whichever monk, out of a desire for the sound of words, plans to go to a great village, or a great city, or a great market-town, or a great hamlet, or a great fortified town, or a great port, or a great capital, or a great mine, or a great caravan station, or a great settlement, or whoever approves of such a monk planning to go—[he commits an offense]. Whichever monk, out of a desire for the sound of words, plans to go to a village-road, or a city-road, up to a settlement-road, or whoever approves of such a monk planning to go—[he commits an offense].

Whichever monk intentionally directs his ear toward the main streets of a village, or the main streets of a town, or even the main streets of a settlement, or whoever approves of one who so directs it; whichever monk intentionally directs his ear toward horse-training grounds, or elephant-training grounds, or training grounds for camels, oxen, buffaloes, or pigs, or whoever approves of one who so directs it.

Whichever monk, out of a desire to hear, attends to or approves of another monk attending to duels with elephants, duels with horses, duels with camels, duels with bulls, duels with buffaloes, or duels with boars; or whichever monk, out of a desire to hear, attends to or approves of another monk attending to chariot-races, horse-races, or elephant-races.

Whichever monk intentionally directs his ear toward places of consecration, or places of storytelling, or places of honorific measurements, or places where there is great music with dancing, singing, instrumental music, stringed instruments, cymbals, hand-clapping, and the sounding of various drums—if he does so himself, or approves of one who does so—he commits an offense.

Whichever monk intentionally directs his ear toward tumults, or riots, or quarrels, or feuds, or great battles, or great conflicts, or strifes, or noisy disputes—if he does so himself, or approves of one who does so—he commits an offense.

Whatever monk, with the intent of listening to sounds, fixes his attention upon various grand festivities where women or men—whether old, middle-aged, or young; whether unadorned or well-adorned; singing, playing instruments, dancing, laughing, sporting, or being intoxicated—are distributing or consuming abundant solid food, soft food, chewables, or tastables; or whoever approves of one who so fixes his attention.

Whatever monk becomes attached, becomes impassioned, becomes infatuated, or becomes obsessed with sounds—whether they belong to this world or the next, whether they have been seen or not seen, heard or not heard, known or not known—if he approves of one who is becoming attached, impassioned, infatuated, or obsessed, then by practicing that, he incurs a four-month period of penance (*parihāra-ṭṭhāna*) that is subject to suspension.
Whichever monk boards a boat for no purpose, or approves of one boarding it, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk buys a boat, has one bought, or boards one that has been brought after being purchased and is being offered to him, or approves of one boarding it, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk boards a boat that has been borrowed, caused to be borrowed, or brought as a loan while it is being offered, or approves of another boarding it; whichever monk boards a boat that has been exchanged, caused to be exchanged, or brought after exchange while it is being offered, or approves of another boarding it;
whichever monk boards a boat that is obtained by seizure, not formally assigned, or brought as a gift while it is being offered, or approves of another boarding it.

Whichever monk causes a boat to be drawn from dry land onto the water, or consents to another doing so; whichever monk causes a boat to be pulled from the water onto dry land, or consents to another doing so; whichever monk bails out a full boat, or consents to another doing so.

Whichever monk, having caused [a boat] to be turned back, boards a boat, or approves of one boarding it; whichever monk, having caused [a boat] to be turned back, boards a boat, or approves of one boarding it;
whichever monk boards a boat going upstream or a boat going downstream, or approves of one boarding it.
Whichever monk boards a boat that travels a *yojana* or half a *yojana*, or approves of one boarding it, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk causes a boat to be pulled out, pushed in, or rowed, or pulls it with a rope, or approves of one doing so, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk rows a boat with a paddle, a shield, a bamboo pole, or a branch, or approves of one rowing it, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk bails out water from a boat with a vessel, an alms-bowl, a cup, or a boat-scoop, or approves of one who is doing so;

whichever monk, having seen a boat being filled with water by a leak and overflowing, covers it with his hand, his foot, a leaf of the *āsattha* tree, a *kusa* blade, clay, or a corner of his robe, or approves of one who is doing so;
whichever monk, while on a boat, accepts food or other requisites from someone on another boat, or approves of one who is doing so.

Whichever monk, while remaining on a boat, accepts food or other requisites from one who is in the water, or approves of another doing so; whichever monk, while remaining on a boat, accepts food or other requisites from one who is in the mud, or approves of another doing so; whichever monk, while remaining on a boat, accepts food or other requisites from one who is on dry land, or approves of another doing so.
Whichever monk, while staying in the water, accepts food or other requisites from one who has come onto a boat, or approves of one so accepting, commits an offense.
Whichever monk, while staying in the water, accepts food or other requisites from one who is also staying in the water, or approves of one so accepting, commits an offense.
Whichever monk, while staying in the water, accepts food or other requisites from one who has gone onto the mud, or approves of one so accepting, commits an offense.
Whichever monk, standing on dry land, accepts food from one who is in the water, or approves of one so accepting;

whichever monk, standing in the mud, accepts food from one who is in a boat, or approves of one so accepting; whichever monk, standing in the mud, accepts food from one who is in the water, or approves of one so accepting.

Whichever monk, being on the mud, accepts food from one who has gone onto the mud, or approves of one who so accepts; whichever monk, being on the mud, accepts food from one who has gone onto dry land, or approves of one who so accepts; whichever monk, being on dry land, accepts food from one who has gone onto a boat, or approves of one who so accepts.

Whichever monk accepts food from one standing on dry land from one who has gone into the water, or approves of one so accepting, commits an offense. Whichever monk accepts food from one standing on dry land from one who has gone into the mud, or approves of one so accepting, commits an offense.
Whichever monk accepts food from one standing on dry land from one who is also standing on dry land, or approves of one so accepting, commits an offense.
Whichever monk buys cloth, has it bought, or accepts cloth being given after it has been brought back from having been bought, or approves of one who so accepts it;
whichever monk borrows cloth, has it borrowed, or accepts cloth being given after it has been brought back from having been borrowed, or approves of one who so accepts it;
whichever monk exchanges cloth, has it exchanged, or accepts cloth being given after it has been brought back from having been exchanged, or approves of one who so accepts it.
Whichever monk accepts a robe that is cut, ungiven, and brought as an offering, or approves of one who so accepts it;

whichever monk, having designated a group and specifically assigned a robe to that group, distributes it to one another without having asked permission from or informed that group, or approves of one who so distributes it.

Whichever monk gives an extra robe to a junior monk or junior nun, or to an elder monk or elder nun—whether they have had their hand cut off, their foot cut off, their ear cut off, their nose cut off, or their lip cut off, or whether they are capable [of providing for themselves]—or whoever approves of such giving;

whichever monk does not give an extra robe to a junior monk or junior nun, or to an elder monk or elder nun—whether they have had their hand cut off up to being incapable [of providing for themselves]—or whoever approves of such non-giving.
Whichever monk wears a robe that is insufficient, unstable, impermanent, or unfit to be worn, or approves of one who so wears it;
whichever monk does not wear a robe that is sufficient, stable, permanent, and fit to be worn, or approves of one who does not so wear it;
whichever monk makes a colored robe colorless, or approves of one who does so.
Whichever monk colors a discolored robe to make it colored, or approves of one who does so;
whichever monk, thinking "I have obtained a new robe," washes or rinses it with cold water or warm water, or approves of one who washes or rinses it;
whichever monk, thinking "I have obtained a new robe," washes or rinses it many times with cold water or warm water, or approves of one who washes or rinses it.
Whichever monk, thinking "I have obtained a new robe," rubs it or scrubs it with *kakkā* (a type of resin), *loddha* (red lead), powder, or dye, or approves of another rubbing or scrubbing it;

whichever monk, thinking "I have obtained a new robe," rubs it or scrubs it with *kakkā*, *loddha*, powder, or dye that has been prepared many days ago, or approves of another rubbing or scrubbing it.
Whichever monk, thinking "I have obtained a foul-smelling cloth," should wash or rinse it with cold water or hot water, or should approve of another washing or rinsing it;

whichever monk, thinking "I have obtained a foul-smelling cloth," should wash or rinse it with cold water or hot water that has been used for many days, or should approve of another washing or rinsing it.

Whichever monk, thinking "I have obtained a foul-smelling cloth," should rub or scrub it with resin, lodhra, powder, or dye, or should approve of one who is rubbing or scrubbing it, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk, thinking "I have obtained a foul-smelling cloth," should rub or scrub it with resin, lodhra, powder, or dye that has been prepared many days ago, or should approve of one who is rubbing or scrubbing it, [commits an offense].

Whichever monk causes a garment to be warmed or heated upon bare ground, or consents to another doing so; whichever monk causes a garment to be warmed or heated upon moist ground, or consents to another doing so; whichever monk causes a garment to be warmed or heated upon ground covered with dust, or consents to another doing so.
Whichever monk causes a cloth to be soaked, or has it soaked, on earth that is smeared with clay, he commits an offense.

Whichever monk causes a cloth to be soaked, or has it soaked, on earth that possesses life, he commits an offense. Whichever monk causes a cloth to be soaked, or has it soaked, on stone that possesses life, he commits an offense.
Whichever monk causes a cloth to be dyed or causes it to be bleached on a piece of leather containing living beings commits an offense;

whichever monk causes a cloth to be dyed or caused to be bleached upon a wooden plank inhabited by living beings—containing eggs, containing creatures, containing seeds, containing sprouts, containing moisture, containing mold, and covered with insects, moss, water-lice, mud, and spiderwebs—commits an offense; or whoever approves of one who so causes it to be dyed or caused to be bleached commits an offense.

Whatever monk should cause a cloth to be dyed or have it dyed on a pillar, a house-beam, a bamboo-pole, a wooden block, or any other such thing produced in the open air that is poorly fastened, poorly placed, unstable, and shaky; or who should approve of another doing so—[he commits an offense].

Whatever monk should cause a cloth to be dyed or have it dyed on a wooden block, a wall, a stone, a brick, or any other such thing produced in the open air that is poorly fixed, poorly placed, unstable, and movable; or should approve of one who is so causing it to be dyed or having it dyed—[he commits an offense].

Whichever monk causes a cloth to be stretched or causes it to be stretched upon a pillar, a wall, a stone, a brick, or any other such thing growing in the open air that is poorly fastened, poorly placed, unstable, and movable, or who approves of one doing so;
whichever monk takes out a cloth from the earth-body, causes it to be taken out, or having had it taken out, accepts it as it is being given, or approves of one doing so.

Whichever monk takes out water-organisms from a cloth, or causes them to be taken out, or accepts them when they are brought back and offered after having been taken out, or approves of one who so accepts them;

whichever monk takes out fire-organisms from a cloth, or causes them to be taken out, or accepts them when they are brought back and offered after having been taken out, or approves of one who so accepts them.

Whichever monk digs up bulbs, roots, leaves, flowers, fruits, or seeds from a dwelling, or causes them to be dug up, or accepts them when they have been dug up and brought to him, or approves of one who so accepts them;
whichever monk digs up medicinal seeds from a dwelling, or causes them to be dug up, or accepts them when they have been dug up and brought to him, or approves of one who so accepts them.

Whichever monk extracts living beings from a cloth, or causes them to be extracted, or accepts it when it is brought back after being extracted and offered to him, or approves of one who so accepts it;
whichever monk shakes out a cloth, or causes it to be shaken out, or accepts it when it is brought back after being shaken out and offered to him, or approves of one who so accepts it;

whichever monk, whether he be a leader or not a leader, a lay follower or not a lay follower, while between villages or on the path between villages, illuminates a cloth and then gives it away, or approves of one who so gives it away.
Whichever monk, having caused a leader, a non-leader, a lay follower, or a non-follower to rise from the midst of the assembly, repeatedly displays his robe, or approves of one who does so;

whichever monk dwells during the summer retreat depending on a robe, or approves of one who so dwells; whichever monk dwells during the rainy season retreat depending on a robe, or approves of one who so dwells.
By practicing that, one incurs a four-month period of penance (*parihāra-ṭṭhāṇa*) with its suspension lifted.
Whichever monk buys cooked food, causes it to be bought, or accepts it when it is brought and given as something already purchased, or approves of one who so accepts it, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk, having borrowed a liquid (*viyaḍa*), causes it to be borrowed, or receives it when it is being given after having been brought back as a loan, or approves of one who so receives it;
whichever monk, having exchanged a liquid, causes it to be exchanged, or receives it when it is being given after having been brought back as an exchange, or approves of one who so receives it;
whichever monk, having received a liquid that was taken by force, not formally assigned, and brought back, receives it when it is being given, or approves of one who so receives it.

Whichever monk accepts more than three mouthfuls of liquid for the sake of one who is ill, or approves of another’s so doing; whichever monk, having taken liquid, travels from village to village, or approves of another’s so doing;
whichever monk boils liquid, causes it to be boiled, or accepts it when it is being offered after having been brought forth by someone else boiling it, or approves of another’s so doing.

Whichever monk recites the *svādhyāya* during four junctions of time, or approves of one who does so, commits an offense; namely: at the morning junction, the evening junction, in the afternoon, and at midnight.

Whichever monk asks more than three questions regarding the *Kālika-śruta*, or approves of one who does so, commits an offense. Whichever monk asks more than seven questions regarding the *Dṛṣṭivāda*, or approves of one who does so, commits an offense.

Whichever monk recites the scriptures during the four great festivals, or approves of one who does so, commits an offense; namely: the festival of Indra, the festival of Khaṇḍa, the festival of the Yakṣas, and the festival of the Bhūtas.

Whichever monk recites the scriptures during the four great full-moon days, or approves of one who does so, commits an offense; namely: the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, the full moon of Āṣāḍha, the full moon of Āśvina, and the full moon of Kārttika.
Whichever monk causes the scripture-recitation to be omitted at the four times of the day, or approves of one who does so, commits an offense.
Whichever monk recites the sacred texts when they are not intended for recitation, or approves of one who does so;

whichever monk recites the sacred texts while his own [text] is not intended for recitation, or approves of one who does so; whichever monk, having not mastered the lower assemblies (*samavasaraṇas*), recites the higher scripture, or approves of one who does so.
Whichever monk, having not mastered the nine stages of celibacy (*nava-brahmacaryāṇi*), teaches the highest scripture (*uttama-śruta*) or approves of one who teaches it;
whichever monk teaches what has not been attained or approves of one who teaches it; whichever monk does not teach what has been attained or does not approve of one who teaches it.

Whichever monk causes an uncompleted recitation to be recited, or approves of one who is causing it to be recited; whichever monk does not cause a completed recitation to be recited, or approves of one who is not causing it to be recited; whichever monk causes an improperly recited portion to be recited, or approves of one who is causing it to be recited.

Whichever monk causes two similar [pupils] to study one [text] while he teaches the other, or approves of one who is teaching [them], [commits an offense]. Whichever monk utters speech not granted by his teachers (ācāryas) or preceptors (upādhyāyas), or approves of one who is uttering it, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk teaches a follower of another sect or a householder, or approves of one who is teaching them, [commits an offense].
Whichever monk receives a follower of another sect or a householder, or approves of one who is receiving them;
whichever monk teaches a *pāsattha* (one who sits at the side), or approves of one who is teaching them; whichever monk receives a *pāsattha*, or approves of one who is receiving them.

Whichever monk teaches what is lax, or approves of one who teaches what is lax; whichever monk receives what is lax, or approves of one who receives what is lax; whichever monk teaches what is indolent, or approves of one who teaches what is indolent.

Whichever monk accepts what is unwholesome, or approves of one who is accepting it; whichever monk teaches what is unwholesome, or approves of one who is teaching it; whichever monk accepts what is unwholesome, or approves of one who is accepting it.
Whichever monk recites mixed [texts], or approves of one who is reciting them; whichever monk receives mixed [texts], or approves of one who is receiving them—
by indulging in that, he incurs a four-month penance involving forfeiture.

Whichever monk, having committed a monthly offense requiring penance, should confess it—confessing without concealment, it is a monthly [penance]; confessing with concealment, it is a two-monthly [penance]. Whichever monk, having committed a two-monthly offense requiring penance, should confess it—confessing without concealment, it is a two-monthly [penance]; confessing with concealment, it is a three-monthly [penance].

If a monk, having committed a three-month penance for an offense, confesses it, [the penalty is] three months if he confesses without concealment, and four months if he confesses with concealment. If a monk, having committed a four-month penance for an offense, confesses it, [the penalty is] four months if he confesses without concealment, and five months if he confesses with concealment.

If a monk, having committed a fault involving a five-month period of penance, confesses it, then for one who confesses without concealment (*apaliuñciya*) it is a five-month penance; for one who confesses with concealment (*paliuñciya*) it is a six-month penance. Beyond that point, whether there was concealment or no concealment, it remains those same six months. If a monk, having repeatedly committed faults involving monthly periods of penance, confesses them, then for one who confesses without concealment it is a one-month penance; for one who confesses with concealment it is a two-month penance.

Whichever monk, having repeatedly committed a two-month penance for an offense, should confess it—confessing without concealment, it is a two-month penance; confessing with concealment, it is a three-month penance.

Whichever monk, having repeatedly committed a three-month penance for an offense, should confess it—confessing without concealment, it is a three-month penance; confessing with concealment, it is a four-month penance.

If a monk, having repeatedly committed a four-month penance (cāummāsiya parihāraṭṭhāṇa), confesses it, for one who confesses without concealment it is a four-month [penance]; for one who confesses with concealment it is five months. If a monk, having repeatedly committed a five-month penance (pañcamāsiya parihāraṭṭhāṇa), confesses it, for one who confesses without concealment it is five months; for one who confesses with concealment it is six months. Beyond that, whether there is concealment or no concealment, it remains those same six months.

If a monk, having committed any one of these grounds for penance—whether it be a monthly, two-monthly, three-monthly, four-monthly, or five-monthly penance—confesses it, then for one who confesses without concealment, the penance is a monthly, two-monthly, three-monthly, four-monthly, or five-monthly penance; for one who confesses with concealment, it is a two-monthly, three-monthly, four-monthly, five-monthly, or six-monthly penance; and beyond that, whether there was concealment or no concealment, it is exactly six months.

Whatever monk, having repeatedly committed any one of these grounds for penance—whether it be a monthly, twice-monthly, three-monthly, four-monthly, or five-monthly penance—should confess it, [if he confesses] without concealment, it is a monthly, twice-monthly, three-monthly, four-monthly, or five-monthly penance; but if he confesses with concealment, it is a twice-monthly, three-monthly, four-monthly, five-monthly, or six-monthly penance. Beyond that, whether there was concealment or no concealment, it is those same six months.

If a monk, having committed any one of these grounds for penance (parihāra-ṭṭhāṇa)—whether it be a four-month penance, more than four months, a five-month penance, or more than five months—and then confesses it, if he confesses without concealment, the penance is four months, more than four months, five months, or more than five months respectively; but if he confesses with concealment, the penance is five months, more than five months, or six months. Beyond that, whether he concealed it or did not conceal it, the penance is exactly those six months.

Whatever monk, having repeatedly committed any one of these grounds for penance—whether it be a four-month penance, or more than four months, or five months, or more than five months—and then confesses it: if he confesses without concealment, it is a four-month penance, or more than four months, or five months, or more than five months; but if he confesses with concealment, it is five months, or more than five months, or six months. Beyond that, whether he concealed it or did not conceal it, it is those same six months.

Whichever monk, having committed any one of these grounds for penance—whether a four-month penance, more than four months, a five-month penance, or more than five months—and having confessed it without concealment, establishes the formal imposition (*ṭhavaṇijja*) and performs the required service (*veyāvaḍiya*); even if he commits [another offense] while under that imposition, he must undergo the full [penalty] right there. [This applies regardless of whether: the offense was committed first and confessed first; the offense was committed first and confessed later; the offense was committed later and confessed first; the offense was committed later and confessed later; [or regarding the state of concealment: confessing without concealment after being unconcealing; confessing with concealment after being unconcealing; confessing without concealment after being concealing; confessing with concealment after being concealing; or confessing without concealment after being unconcealing. For one who confesses in this way, all of this, having been combined with what was personally done, if he commits another offense while undergoing the penance established by this procedure, he must undergo the full [penalty] right there.

If a monk, having repeatedly committed any one of these grounds for penance—whether it be a four-month penance, more than four months, a five-month penance, or more than five months—and having confessed it without concealment, should be placed under formal supervision (*ṭhavaṇijja*) and required to perform service (*veyāvaḍiya*); yet even after being so supervised, he commits another offense, he must undergo the full [penalty] right there. Whether the offense was committed first and confessed first; or the offense was committed first and confessed later; or the offense was committed later and confessed first; or the offense was committed later and confessed later; whether he confesses without concealment after not concealing; or without concealment after concealing; or concealing after not concealing; or concealing after concealing; or without concealment after not concealing—if he confesses all this by combining what he has done, and if, while undergoing the formal placement (*paṭṭhavaṇā*), he commits another offense, he too must undergo the full [penalty] right there.

If a monk, having committed any one of these grounds for penance (parihāra-ṭṭhāṇa)—whether it be a four-month penance, more than four months, a five-month penance, or more than five months—and then confesses it while concealing it, he must be placed under formal restriction (ṭhavaṇijja) and service (veyāvaḍiya) must be performed for him. Even after being placed under restriction, if he commits another offense, that too must be fully undergone right there. Whether the offense was committed first and confessed first; the offense was committed first and confessed later; the offense was committed later and confessed first; or the offense was committed later and confessed later; whether he concealed it or did not conceal it when he did not conceal it; whether he concealed it when he did not conceal it; whether he concealed it when he did conceal it; or whether he concealed it when he concealed it—if he confesses all of this by combining what was done by himself, and if he commits an offense while undergoing the probationary period (nivvisamāṇe) established by such a formal procedure, that too must be fully undergone right there.

If a monk, having repeatedly committed any one of these grounds for penance—whether it be a four-month penance, more than four months, a five-month penance, or more than five months—and having confessed it while concealing [the offense], should be placed under formal suspension (*ṭhavaṇijja*); and even after being so suspended, if he commits another offense, that entire [period] must be undergone right there. [Regarding the sequence: 1. First committed, first confessed; 2. First committed, later confessed; 3. Later committed, first confessed; 4. Later committed, later confessed; 5. Without concealment, first committed, first confessed; 6. Without concealment, first committed, later confessed; 7. Without concealment, later committed, first confessed; 8. Without concealment, later committed, later confessed; 9. With concealment, first committed, first confessed; 10. With concealment, first committed, later confessed; 11. With concealment, later committed, first confessed; 12. With concealment, later committed, later confessed. For one who confesses while concealing [the offense], all this must be combined with what was personally done, and whoever, having been placed under such a formal suspension, commits [another offense] while undergoing the penance, that entire [period] must be undergone right there.

When a naked ascetic (anagāra) has been assigned a six-month period of penance (parihāraṭṭhāṇa), if he should, in the interim, commit a fault requiring a two-month period of penance and confess it—provided that the subsequent imposition of the penalty (ārōvaṇā) for the twenty-night offense is with its beginning, middle, and end, together with its purpose, its cause, and its reason, neither deficient nor excessive—then beyond that, the total duration shall be two months plus twenty nights.

If a homeless ascetic (anagāra), having been assigned a five-month penance (parihāraṭṭhāṇa), should in the interim commit a two-month offense and confess it, there is another imposition of twenty nights (ārōvaṇā) at the beginning, middle, and end, with its purpose, reason, and cause, neither deficient nor excessive; beyond that, it is two months plus twenty nights.

If a naked ascetic (anagāra) who has been assigned a four-month penance (parihāra-ṭṭhāṇa) should, in the interim, commit a two-month offense and confess it, there is another imposition of twenty nights (ārōvaṇā) at the beginning, middle, and end—provided with its purpose, its cause, and its reason, neither deficient nor excessive; beyond that, it is two months plus twenty nights.

When an ascetic has been assigned a three-month penance, if he commits another offense during that period requiring a two-month penance and confesses it, there is a further imposition of twenty nights; this applies to the beginning, middle, or end [of the original term], provided it is with purpose, with reason, and with cause, being neither deficient nor excessive. Beyond that, the total duration is two months plus twenty nights.

When a naked ascetic (anagāra) has been assigned a two-month penance (parihāraṭṭhāṇa), if he commits an offense during that period and confesses it, there is another imposition of twenty nights (ārōvaṇā) at the beginning, middle, or end, provided it is with purpose, with reason, and with cause—neither deficient nor excessive. Beyond that, the [original] two months plus the twenty nights [are to be observed].

When a homeless ascetic has been assigned a one-month penance (*parihāra-ṭṭhāṇa*) and, in the interim, commits a two-month offense and confesses it, there is another twenty-night imposition (*ārōvaṇā*) at the beginning, middle, and end, with its purpose, reason, and cause, neither deficient nor excessive; beyond that, it is two months plus twenty nights.

When a homeless ascetic has been assigned a two-month period of penance (*parihāraṭṭhāṇa*) consisting of twenty nights, and in the interim he commits another offense for which a two-month penance is prescribed, he should confess it. There is another twenty-night imposition (*ārōvaṇā*) at the beginning, middle, and end, with its purpose, reason, and cause, neither deficient nor excessive; beyond that, there are ten nights and three months. For a three-month penance, including the ten nights, up to that point, there are four months.
For a four-month penance, including the twenty nights, there are four months.
A four-month period of penance (*parihāra-ṭṭhāṇa*) plus twenty nights, up to that point; beyond that, it is one hundred and sixty nights, which is five months.

When a five-month period of penance plus one hundred and sixty nights has been assigned, if a *anagāra* (homeless ascetic) should, in the interim, commit a two-month period of penance and then confess it—there is another imposition of twenty nights at the beginning, middle, and end, with its purpose, its reason, and its cause, neither deficient nor excessive; beyond that, it is six months.
A six-month period of penance, up to that point; beyond that, it is one month and a half.
A five-month penance period, up to one month and a half beyond that;
a four-month penance period, up to one month and a half beyond that;
a three-month penance period, up to one month and a half beyond that.
A two-month period of penance (*parihāra-ṭṭhāṇa*) up to one and a half months [may be assigned]. When a one-month period of penance has been assigned, up to one and a half months [may be added].

When a one-and-a-half-month period of penance has been assigned, if an ascetic (*anagāra*) should in the interim commit a one-month offense and confess it, there is another fortnightly imposition (*pakkhiyā ārōvaṇā*) at the beginning, middle, and end—along with its purpose, its reason, and its cause—which is neither deficient nor excessive; beyond that, it is two months.
When a naked ascetic (anagāra) has been assigned a two-month penance (parihāraṭṭhāṇa), and thereafter [another offense occurs] within two and a half months;

if that naked ascetic, having been assigned a two-and-a-half-month penance, commits in the interim a one-month penance and confesses it—provided there is another fortnightly imposition (pakkhiyā ārōvaṇā) at the beginning, middle, and end, with its own purpose, reason, and cause, neither deficient nor excessive—then beyond that, the maximum is three months.

If a monk who has been assigned a three-month period of penance (*parihāra-ṭṭhāṇa*) should, in the interim, commit another offense for which a one-month penance is prescribed and confess it, there is another fortnightly imposition (*ārōvaṇā*) at the beginning, middle, and end, with its purpose, reason, and cause, neither deficient nor excessive; beyond that, [the maximum is] four and a half months.

If a monk who has been assigned a four-and-a-half-month period of penance should [commit another offense], beyond that [the maximum is] four months. If a monk who has been assigned a four-month period of penance should [commit another offense], beyond that [the maximum is] four and a half months.

When a place of penance lasting four and a half months has been assigned to an ascetic, it lasts for up to five months beyond that. When a place of penance lasting five months has been assigned to an ascetic, it lasts for up to five and a half months beyond that. When a place of penance lasting five and a half months has been assigned, it lasts for up to six months beyond that.
When a mendicant has been assigned a two-month penance, and after that period he commits another offense, he may be assigned a two-and-a-half-month penance.

If a mendicant who has been assigned a two-and-a-half-month penance confesses after having committed a two-month penance in the interim, there is a further imposition of twenty nights, beginning, middle, and end, with its purpose, reason, and cause, neither deficient nor excessive; beyond that, it is three months plus five nights.

If a monk who has been assigned a month-long penance (*parihāra-ṭṭhāṇa*) for five nights commits another offense during that period, he should confess it. Furthermore, there is a fortnightly imposition (*ārōvaṇā*): at the beginning, middle, or end, with its purpose, reason, and cause, neither deficient nor excessive; beyond that, it lasts for three months plus twenty days.

If a naked ascetic (anagāra), having been assigned a probationary period (parihāraṭṭhāṇa) of one month and twenty nights, should in the interim commit an offense requiring a probationary period of two months and then confess it, there is another assignment of twenty nights for the confession, beginning, middle, and end, with its purpose, its cause, and its reason—neither deficient nor excessive; beyond that, for up to ten days, there are four months [of probation].

When a naked ascetic (anagāra) has been assigned a four-month period of penance for a transgression, if he commits an intermediate monthly penance and confesses it—provided that the subsequent fortnightly imposition of penance is with its beginning, middle, and end, with its purpose, its reason, and its cause, neither deficient nor excessive—then beyond that, there may be up to five months less five days.

When a homeless ascetic (anagāra) has been assigned a probationary period (parihāraṭṭhāṇa) of four months and five days, and in the interim commits another offense requiring a probationary period of two months, he should confess it. There is another imposition of twenty nights (ārōvaṇā), beginning, middle, and end, with its purpose, its cause, and its reason, neither deficient nor excessive; beyond that, it is for five and a half months.

When a homeless ascetic has been assigned a *parihāra-sthāna* (penance) for five and a half months, if he should commit an intermediate *māsa-parihāra-sthāna* offense and confess it, there is another fortnightly imposition (*pakkhiyā ārovaṇā*) at the beginning, middle, and end, with its purpose, its cause, and its reason, neither deficient nor excessive; beyond that, [the maximum is] six months.
